metadata.title: Welcome and starter
metadata.summary: Meet the unit, then choose one emerging technology example.

content.text: Welcome
This unit is Exploring New and Emerging Digital Technologies (M/618/3683). Across the year you will outline technologies, then explain how people and organisations use them.

Digital technology changes quickly. Businesses that spot useful new tools early can improve service, cut cost or stay safe. This lesson is formative practice for LO1 / AC 1.1. It is not Gateway assignment evidence.

content.title: By the end of this lesson
content.text: Define digital technology. Tell current from emerging. Outline mobile, intelligent computing, IoT and cloud. Spot simple business uses.

Misconception: learners often treat any new phone as emerging. Extension: ask for one sector where a current tool is still emerging. Discussion: why must businesses adapt? Differentiation: pair write the starter before sharing.
Starter

feedback.incorrect: Emerging technology is still developing or not yet widely used. A common office PC or projector is current.

metadata.title: What is digital technology?
metadata.summary: Outline devices, software, networks and data, then match each description to a technology.

content.text: What is digital technology?
Digital technology uses electronic devices and software to create, store, share or process data.
Devices are the hardware, such as phones, sensors and servers. Software is the programs and apps that tell hardware what to do.
Networks connect devices so they can share data. Data is the information those systems collect, such as a location, a payment or a temperature reading.

metadata.title: Current versus emerging
metadata.summary: Explain the difference, then sort examples.

content.text: Current vs emerging technologies
Current technology is already in common use. Most people or organisations in that setting already rely on it.
Emerging technology is still developing, is costly, or is not yet widely adopted. The same product can be current in one sector and emerging in another.
Example: contactless payment is current in many UK shops. A consumer brain-computer headset is still emerging.
Ask: would most people in this setting already use it this year?

content.text: Mobile technology
Mobile technology is computing you can carry. Smartphones and tablets run apps for messaging, maps, learning and work.
Mobile payments let people tap a phone or watch to pay. GPS gives location for maps, deliveries and safety.
Mobile banking lets customers check balances, pay bills and approve logins without a branch visit.

metadata.title: Intelligent computing
metadata.summary: Outline AI, machine learning, automation and robotics, then judge five statements.

content.text: Intelligent computing
Intelligent computing is software and machines that can perform tasks that used to need human judgement, such as spotting a pattern or choosing a next step.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is the broad idea. Machine learning is a common method: the system improves by training on examples rather than only following fixed rules.
Automation runs a process with little human input, such as sorting invoices. Robotics uses machines that move or handle objects, sometimes with AI to decide what to do next.
True or false

options.label: True
False

feedback.correct: Machine learning trains on data so the system can improve without rewriting every rule by hand.
feedback.incorrect: Machine learning trains on data so the system can improve without rewriting every rule by hand.

feedback.incorrect: Automation is often used for repeated processes such as copying invoice data.

content.text: Internet of Things
The Internet of Things (IoT) is a network of physical devices that collect or share data, often with little manual input.
Smart homes use connected lights, speakers and thermostats. Wearables such as a fitness watch are IoT when they send health or activity data.
Industrial IoT uses sensors and machines in warehouses and factories to track stock, temperature or equipment.

metadata.title: Cloud technology
metadata.summary: Outline SaaS, IaaS and PaaS, then complete each sentence.

content.text: Cloud technology
Cloud technology delivers computing over the internet instead of only from one local device. Users can often scale up or down as they need.
SaaS is software you use in a browser or app, such as email. IaaS rents infrastructure such as virtual machines and storage. PaaS gives a ready place to build and run applications.

content.title: Keep it simple
content.text: Ask who manages the application. If the provider runs the app for you, it is usually SaaS.

metadata.title: IoT and connected devices
metadata.summary: Outline what IoT is and what makes a device 'connected'.

content.text: IoT and connected devices
IoT devices sense, act or share data with little manual input. A connected device can send or receive data over a network (Wi-Fi, mobile, Bluetooth or similar).
Examples: smart thermostat, warehouse temperature sensor, connected street light, hospital infusion pump that reports status.

content.prompt: A device is 'connected' mainly when it can:

feedback.incorrect: Connected devices exchange data over a network.

metadata.title: RFID principles
metadata.summary: Outline how RFID tags and readers identify items.

content.text: RFID
RFID uses radio tags and readers to identify items. Readers can often scan tags without lining every item up under a camera, which helps stock and asset tracking.
Typical uses: clothing tags in retail, pallet tags in warehouses, library books, tool tracking on a site.

content.prompt: RFID is most useful when an organisation needs to:

options.label: Identify tagged items at short distance without lining each one under a camera

Project a hologram in a classroom
Run a spreadsheet with no tags

feedback.correct: RFID readers identify tagged items at short range, including when items are not lined up one by one.
feedback.incorrect: RFID readers identify tagged items at short range, including when items are not lined up one by one.

metadata.title: NFC principles
metadata.summary: Outline NFC as very short-range radio for secure taps.

content.text: NFC
NFC (Near Field Communication) is very short-range radio, usually centimetres. It suits short taps such as contactless payment, door badges and ticket gates.

metadata.title: Benefits, risks and security
metadata.summary: Check benefits of connected tech and key security risks.

content.text: Benefits, risks and security
Benefits include automation, better decisions from live data, and convenience. Risks include hacking, outages, cost, and poor configuration.

feedback.incorrect: Weak credentials and missing updates are common IoT security risks.

content.text: Privacy and real-world cases
Wearables and healthcare IoT often handle sensitive data. Organisations need consent, clear purpose, access control and secure storage.

content.text: Welcome to Week 4
This week you outline artificial intelligence (AI) and intelligent computing: smart devices, robots and neural networks (AC1.1).

content.title: By the end of this week
content.text: You will be able to explain what AI is and is not. You will describe how smart devices and robots sense, decide and act. You will outline how a neural network learns from examples. You will weigh up the benefits and limitations of AI in real situations.
First, a quick recap of Week 3. Ask what the customer is getting: a ready app (SaaS), a platform to build apps (PaaS), rented infrastructure (IaaS) or a remote desktop (DaaS).

content.prompt: Match each Week 3 example to its cloud service model.

items.text: A class uses a browser-based spreadsheet with nothing to install
An IT team rents virtual servers and installs its own operating system

feedback.correct: Well recalled. SaaS gives you a ready app. IaaS rents raw infrastructure such as virtual servers that you manage yourself.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Ask what is being provided. A ready-to-use app is SaaS. Rented servers you manage yourself are IaaS.

content.prompt: Many AI services, such as voice assistants, send your request to powerful remote servers to be processed. Which Week 3 idea does this link to?

options.label: Cloud computing: processing happens on remote servers reached over the internet
Local storage: everything happens only on the device
DaaS: the assistant gives you a full remote desktop
IaaS: the speaker rents you your own virtual server to manage

feedback.correct: Correct. Many AI features rely on the cloud because training and running AI can need more computing power than a phone or speaker has.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. The request is sent over the internet to cloud servers, where the heavy processing happens. You are not given a desktop (DaaS) or a server to manage (IaaS), and the work does not stay only on the device.

metadata.title: What is AI?
metadata.summary: Define artificial intelligence and compare it with rule-based software.

content.text: What is AI?
Artificial intelligence (AI) lets computers do tasks that normally need human intelligence. Examples are recognising a face, understanding speech or predicting what might happen next.

Rule-based software is different. It follows fixed instructions written by a programmer: "if this happens, do that". It does the same thing every time and cannot improve on its own. A calculator and a timer are rule-based.

Many AI systems use machine learning. The programmer does not write every rule. Instead, the system is trained on lots of examples and finds patterns in them. It can then deal with new data it has not seen before.
AI can be very good at spotting patterns, but it does not think, understand or feel like a person.

content.title: Not all software is AI
content.text: Most software is rule-based. Software only counts as AI when it recognises patterns, learns from data or makes predictions. Being automatic or clever-looking is not enough.

content.prompt: Which statement best defines artificial intelligence?

options.label: Any program that runs on a computer
Technology that lets computers do tasks that normally need human intelligence, such as recognising patterns or making predictions
A computer that has feelings and thinks exactly like a person
Software that only follows a fixed list of instructions

feedback.correct: Correct. AI is about carrying out tasks that usually need human intelligence, such as recognising patterns, understanding language or making predictions.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Not every program is AI, and AI does not have feelings or think like a person. A fixed list of instructions describes rule-based software. AI handles tasks that normally need human intelligence, such as spotting patterns or making predictions.

content.prompt: A spam filter improves over time as it sees thousands of emails that people mark as spam. A different filter only blocks emails containing the exact word "prize". Which is the better description?

options.label: Both filters are AI because they both block emails
The first filter learns from examples (AI); the second follows one fixed rule (rule-based)
The second filter is AI because it has a rule
Neither filter is software

feedback.correct: Correct. The first filter learns patterns from labelled examples, which is machine learning. The second follows a fixed rule a programmer wrote, so it is rule-based software.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Doing a useful job does not make software AI. The filter that learns from thousands of labelled emails is AI (machine learning). The filter that only checks for one exact word follows a fixed rule, so it is rule-based.

metadata.title: AI in everyday life
metadata.summary: Recognise everyday examples of AI: recommendations, voice assistants, image recognition, navigation, spam detection and game AI.

content.text: AI in everyday life
You probably use AI every day without noticing. Here are six common examples.
Recommendations: streaming and shopping sites suggest films or products based on what you, and people like you, chose before.
Voice assistants: smart speakers and phones recognise spoken words and work out what you want.
Image recognition: phones group photos by faces, and apps can identify a plant from a picture.
Navigation: map apps use data from thousands of journeys to predict traffic and suggest faster routes.
Spam detection: email services learn what junk mail usually looks like and filter it out.
Game AI: some computer-controlled characters learn from how you play and change their tactics.

content.prompt: A map app suggests a new route because it predicts heavy traffic ahead, based on data from thousands of other journeys. What is the AI doing?

options.label: Recognising patterns in large amounts of data to make a prediction
Printing a paper map
Following one fixed route that never changes
Storing the map on a USB stick

feedback.correct: Correct. The app spots patterns in lots of journey data and predicts where traffic will build up. Pattern recognition and prediction are typical AI tasks.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. A route that never changes would be rule-based. The app is using lots of journey data to spot patterns and predict traffic, which is what makes it AI.

metadata.title: AI or not AI?
metadata.summary: Classify examples as AI or not AI to show that not all software is AI.

content.text: AI or not AI?
Ask: does it learn from data, recognise patterns or make predictions? If it only follows fixed steps that a programmer set, it is not AI, even if it happens automatically.

content.prompt: For each example, choose AI or Not AI.

items.text: A phone unlocks after recognising the owner's face
A calculator app adds two numbers
A music app builds a playlist from your listening habits

feedback.correct: Correct. Face unlock and playlists recognise patterns or learn from data. A calculator just follows set rules.
feedback.incorrect: Some are not right yet. Being automatic is not the same as being AI. A calculator follows rules set by a person. AI recognises patterns or learns from data, such as recognising a face.

metadata.title: How smart devices work
metadata.summary: Describe the smart system flow: sensors, data, processing, then a decision or action.

content.text: How smart devices work
A smart device senses the world around it and responds. Most follow the same four-step flow: Sensors → Data → Processing → Decision or action.
1. Sensors measure something, such as temperature, movement, sound, light or heart rate.
2. The measurements are stored as data (usually numbers).
3. Processing: the device, or a cloud service, checks the data and works out what it means.
4. Decision or action: the device does something, such as turning the heating on or sending an alert.
Examples: a smart thermostat, a smartwatch, a smart speaker, a smart doorbell camera and smart lighting.

content.title: Smart does not always mean AI
content.text: Some smart devices follow a simple rule, such as a light that switches off after ten minutes with no movement. Others use AI, such as a thermostat that learns your weekly routine. Ask: does it only follow a rule, or does it learn or recognise patterns?

content.prompt: In a smart thermostat, which part is the sensor?

options.label: The temperature sensor that measures how warm the room is
The boiler turning on
The app on your phone
The heating schedule saved in the thermostat

feedback.correct: Correct. The temperature sensor measures the room. Its readings become data that the thermostat processes before deciding whether to switch the heating on.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. The boiler turning on is the action at the end of the flow, and a saved schedule is stored data. The sensor is the part that measures the world: here, the temperature sensor.

content.prompt: A smart light switches off when nobody has moved in a room for ten minutes. Which part of the flow is "switching off"?

options.label: Sensor
Data
Processing
Decision or action

feedback.correct: Correct. Switching off is the action. This light follows one simple rule (no movement for ten minutes means switch off), so it is smart but does not need AI.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. The motion sensor detects movement (sensor), its readings are stored (data), and they are checked (processing). Switching the light off is the final decision or action.

metadata.title: Order the smart system flow
metadata.summary: Put the steps of a smart system in the correct order.

content.text: Order the smart system flow
A smartwatch warns its wearer when their heart rate is unusually high while they are sitting still. The four things the watch does are listed below in the wrong order.

content.prompt: Put the watch's actions in order. For each one, choose Step 1 (happens first) to Step 4 (happens last). Use each step once.

items.text: The watch vibrates and shows a warning on the screen
A light on the back of the watch detects the wearer's pulse
The watch checks the numbers against the wearer's usual resting heart rate
Each pulse measurement is saved as a number, such as 118 beats per minute

feedback.correct: Correct order. The watch senses the pulse, saves it as data, processes it by comparing with normal, then acts with a warning. That is Sensors → Data → Processing → Decision or action.
feedback.incorrect: Not in the right order yet. A smart system must sense something before it has any data. It can only check data it has already saved. The warning is the action, so it comes last.

metadata.title: IoT and AI: not the same thing
metadata.summary: Link to Week 2: IoT and AI can work together, but they are not the same thing.

content.text: IoT and AI: not the same thing
In Week 2 you met the Internet of Things (IoT): everyday devices that connect to the internet and share data. IoT is about connecting and sharing.
AI is about learning from data, recognising patterns and making predictions.
A device can be IoT without any AI, such as a smart plug you switch on from an app. When IoT and AI work together, the connected devices collect the data and AI makes sense of it.

content.prompt: Which statement about IoT and AI is correct?

options.label: IoT and AI mean exactly the same thing
Every IoT device uses AI
IoT connects devices to share data; AI can analyse that data. They can work together but are different
AI only works without the internet

feedback.correct: Correct. IoT is about connected devices sharing data. AI is about learning from data and making decisions. Together, IoT can collect the data and AI can find patterns in it.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Many IoT devices simply send readings or respond to app commands with no AI at all. IoT connects and shares data; AI learns from data. They often work together, but they are not the same.

content.prompt: For each connected device, choose IoT only or IoT and AI together.

categories.label: IoT and AI together (also learns or recognises)

items.text: A smart plug you switch on remotely from a phone app
A thermostat that learns your weekly routine and adjusts the heating
A doorbell camera that recognises the difference between a person and a parcel

feedback.correct: Correct. Responding to app commands is IoT only. Learning routines or recognising images adds AI.
feedback.incorrect: Some are not right yet. Ask: does the device only connect and share data, or does it also learn, recognise or predict? A remote plug is IoT only. Recognising a person in a camera image needs AI.

metadata.title: What is a robot?
metadata.summary: Describe robots in terms of sensors, a controller and actuators, and compare programmed and AI-enabled behaviour.

content.text: What is a robot?
A robot is a machine that can sense its surroundings and carry out physical actions. Most robots have three main parts.
Sensors take information in, for example cameras, bump sensors and distance sensors.
The controller is the robot's computer. It runs the program and decides what to do.
Actuators make the robot move or do physical work, for example motors, wheels, grippers and arms.

Programmed behaviour means the robot follows fixed steps, such as a factory arm welding the same spot on every car. AI-enabled behaviour means the robot can recognise things and adapt, such as a delivery robot spotting an obstacle and finding a way round it.
Robots are used in manufacturing, warehouses, homes (robot vacuums), deliveries, self-driving vehicles and hospitals, where they can help surgeons or carry medicines between wards.

content.title: A robot is not automatically AI
content.text: Many robots just repeat programmed movements very accurately. A robot only uses AI if it can learn, recognise or adapt, for example by recognising objects with a camera.

content.prompt: Which part of a robot makes it physically move, for example its wheels or gripper?

options.label: Sensor
Controller
Actuator
Data

feedback.correct: Correct. Actuators, such as motors, wheels and grippers, turn the controller's decisions into physical movement.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Sensors gather information and the controller decides what to do. The parts that actually move, such as motors, wheels and grippers, are actuators.

content.prompt: A factory robot arm places a lid on every jar in exactly the same way, all day. Which is true?

options.label: It must be AI because it is a robot
It is a robot following programmed behaviour, so it does not need AI
It is not a robot because it does not walk
It is IoT because it is in a factory

feedback.correct: Correct. Repeating the same programmed movement is robotics without AI. Robots only use AI when they need to recognise, learn or adapt.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Being a robot does not make something AI, and robots do not need to walk. This arm follows the same programmed steps each time, so it is robotics without AI.

metadata.title: Match robot parts to their role
metadata.summary: Match robot components to sensor, controller or actuator.

content.text: Match robot parts to their role
A robot vacuum cleaner has several parts. Sensors take information in, the controller decides, and actuators act.

content.prompt: Match each robot vacuum part to its role: Sensor, Controller or Actuator.

items.text: Bump sensor on the front edge
Motors that turn the wheels
Onboard computer running the cleaning program
Spinning brush that sweeps up dust

feedback.correct: Correct. The bump sensor takes information in. The onboard computer decides. Wheel motors and brushes carry out the actions.
feedback.incorrect: Some are not right yet. If a part gathers information, it is a sensor. If it decides, it is the controller. If it moves or does physical work, it is an actuator.

metadata.title: Predetermined automation or AI-enabled?
metadata.summary: Classify behaviours as predetermined automation or AI-enabled behaviour.

content.text: Predetermined automation or AI-enabled?
Automation means a machine or program does a job without a person doing it by hand.
Predetermined means decided in advance. Predetermined automation follows steps that a person set up, and does the same thing every time the same thing happens.
AI-enabled behaviour can cope with new situations by recognising patterns or learning from data.

content.title: Automation is not the same as AI
content.text: A machine can be fully automatic and still use no AI at all. Using a sensor does not make something AI either: automatic doors use a sensor but always do the same thing.

content.prompt: For each behaviour, choose Predetermined automation or AI-enabled behaviour.

items.text: A car-wash machine runs the same wash cycle for every car
A delivery robot recognises a dog on the pavement and steers around it
Automatic doors open whenever the motion sensor is triggered
A self-driving car predicts that a cyclist is about to turn and slows down

feedback.correct: Correct. Fixed cycles and sensor-triggered doors are predetermined. Recognising objects and predicting what people will do are AI-enabled.
feedback.incorrect: Some are not right yet. Ask: would it behave exactly the same way every time? If yes, it is predetermined, even if it uses a sensor like the automatic doors. AI-enabled behaviour recognises, learns or predicts.

metadata.title: What is a neural network?
metadata.summary: Outline a neural network as inputs passing through connected nodes to produce an output.

content.text: What is a neural network?
A neural network is a type of AI that is especially good at recognising patterns, such as spotting a cat in a photo.
It is made of many small processing units called nodes. The nodes are connected to each other and arranged in rows called layers.
It works in three stages: Inputs → Connected nodes → Output.
Inputs: the data goes in. For a photo, this is the colour of each tiny dot (pixel) in the picture.
Connected nodes: the data passes through the layers. Early layers pick out simple patterns, such as edges. Later layers combine these into bigger features, such as ears or whiskers.
Output: the network gives its answer, such as "cat: 92% likely".
A network can only do this after it has been trained on lots of examples. You will see how training works shortly.

content.title: Common misconception
content.text: The idea of connected nodes was loosely inspired by brain cells, but a neural network is not a brain. It does not understand, think or feel like a person. It finds patterns in data, and only the kinds of patterns it has been trained on.

content.prompt: Which description best matches a neural network?

options.label: Inputs pass through layers of connected nodes to produce an output
A cable network that connects computers in an office
A human brain placed inside a computer
A list of fixed if-then rules written by a programmer

feedback.correct: Correct. A neural network takes inputs, passes them through layers of connected nodes that pick out patterns, and produces an output.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Despite the word "network", it has nothing to do with cables between computers, and it is not a real brain. It is also not a list of fixed rules: it learns patterns from examples. The structure is inputs → connected nodes → output.

content.prompt: A friend says: "Neural networks think and understand just like humans do." What is the best response?

options.label: That is true; they have feelings too
That is not accurate: they find patterns in data they have been trained on but do not think or understand like people
That is true, but only on smartphones
Neural networks cannot do anything useful

feedback.correct: Correct. Neural networks are loosely inspired by the brain, but they are pattern-finding tools. They do not understand meaning, have feelings or use human judgement.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Neural networks are useful, but they do not think, understand or feel. They find patterns in the data they were trained on, and can get things badly wrong outside that data.

metadata.title: Order the neural network flow
metadata.summary: Order the steps a trained neural network follows when it identifies a new photo.

content.text: Order the neural network flow
A neural network that has already been trained to recognise animals is given a new photo. What happens inside it is listed below in the wrong order.

content.prompt: Put the stages in order. For each one, choose Step 1 (happens first) to Step 4 (happens last). Use each step once.

items.text: Later layers combine those patterns into features such as ears and whiskers
The colour of each pixel in the photo goes in as input data
The network gives its answer: "cat: 92% likely"
Early layers of connected nodes pick out simple patterns, such as edges

feedback.correct: Correct order. Inputs, then connected nodes finding simple patterns, then bigger features, then the output. The answer always comes last.
feedback.incorrect: Not in the right order yet. The photo has to go in as input data first. Simple patterns such as edges are found before bigger features such as ears. The answer (the output) comes last.

metadata.title: How a neural network learns
metadata.summary: Explain training with a cat and dog example, and why good data matters.

content.text: How a neural network learns
Training is how a neural network learns. For example, you might teach one to tell cats from dogs.
1. People collect thousands of photos and label each one "cat" or "dog".
2. The network looks at a photo and guesses. At first, its guesses are almost random.
3. It is told the correct label and adjusts its connections a little, so it is more likely to be right next time. This repeats thousands of times.
4. It is tested on photos it has never seen. If it does well, it has learned general patterns, not just memorised the training photos.

content.title: Data matters, and mistakes still happen
content.text: A network can only learn from the examples it is given. If the training photos are limited or unbalanced, its answers will be too. Even a well-trained network still gets some answers wrong, for example a fluffy dog in a dark photo.

content.prompt: A network was trained only on photos of ginger cats. It then fails to recognise a black cat. What is the most likely reason?

options.label: Black cats are not really cats
The training data was too limited, so it never learned what other cats look like
The network was switched off
Neural networks cannot recognise animals

feedback.correct: Correct. The network only learned from ginger cats, so it did not learn that cats can be other colours. Varied, balanced training data leads to better results.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Neural networks can recognise animals, but only from patterns in their training data. With only ginger cats to learn from, the network has never seen what a black cat looks like.

metadata.title: Benefits and limitations of AI
metadata.summary: Classify benefits and limitations of AI and intelligent computing.

content.text: Benefits and limitations of AI
Benefits. AI can:
work very fast, automate repetitive tasks, analyse huge amounts of data (often called big data), give consistent results, spot patterns people might miss, and work day and night without breaks.
Limitations. AI:

is only as good as its data, can make mistakes, and can be biased (unfair to some groups) if its training data was unbalanced. It can be expensive to build and run, and it can raise privacy concerns because it often collects personal data. It also lacks human judgement, empathy and common sense.

content.title: Spotting patterns is not the same as judgement
content.text: An AI can recognise patterns very well and still make a poor decision in an unusual situation, because it does not understand people's circumstances the way a person does.

content.prompt: For each statement, choose Benefit or Limitation.

items.text: Checks thousands of bank transactions per second
Gives unfair results if its training data was biased

feedback.correct: Correct. Speed is a benefit. Bias from unfair training data is a limitation.
feedback.incorrect: Some are not right yet. Benefits are things AI does well, such as speed. Limitations include bias from data.

metadata.title: Scenario: Pixel Forge Games: an NPC that adapts
metadata.summary: Decide whether two adapting Pixel Forge Games characters use AI, and what data an AI character learns from.

content.text: Scenario: Pixel Forge Games: an NPC that adapts
Pixel Forge Games is designing a fighting game. A non-player character (NPC) is controlled by the computer. Two trial versions both have an enemy NPC that changes as you play.
Version A: the designers wrote a rule. If you lose three fights in a row, the enemy's health drops by 20%.
Version B: over many fights, the enemy notices that you usually attack from the left. It starts guarding its left side and tries new tactics you have not seen before.

content.prompt: Both enemies change as you play. Which one shows AI-enabled behaviour?

options.label: Version A, because it changes the difficulty automatically
Version B, because it recognises patterns in how you play and adapts to them
Both, because anything that adapts is AI
Neither, because games cannot use AI

feedback.correct: Correct. Version B spots a pattern in your play and responds to it. Version A only follows a rule the designers wrote in advance, so it is automatic but not AI.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Changing automatically is not the same as AI. Version A follows one fixed rule the designers wrote (three losses means less health). Version B recognises a pattern in how you fight and adapts, which is AI-enabled behaviour.

content.prompt: What data does the Version B enemy need to learn from?

options.label: Records of your moves in past fights, such as which side you attack from
The game's fixed rule about losing three fights
Your screen brightness setting
The make of your games console

feedback.correct: Correct. To spot your habits, the enemy needs data about what you actually do in fights, collected over many games.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. A fixed rule is what Version A uses, not something to learn from, and screen settings or the console make say nothing about how you fight. To learn your habits, the enemy needs records of your moves.

metadata.title: Scenario: Pixel Forge Games: a smart gaming setup
metadata.summary: Select which data a Pixel Forge Games smart setup needs and identify a privacy concern.

content.text: Scenario: Pixel Forge Games: a smart gaming setup
Pixel Forge Games is testing a smart gaming setup with three jobs:
1. Change the colour of the room lights to match what is happening in the game.
2. Dim the lights when the room is bright.
3. Turn the game volume down when someone speaks to the player.
A well-designed device should only collect the data it needs for its jobs. Collecting extra personal data creates privacy risks.

content.prompt: Which data does the setup need? For each item, choose Needed if one of the three jobs cannot work without it, or Not needed if none of the jobs uses it.

items.text: Game events, such as an explosion or a boss battle starting
Light level readings from a light sensor in the room
Full recordings of everything said in the room, stored online

feedback.correct: Correct. Game events and light readings are needed for the lighting jobs. Storing full recordings online is not needed for any job and creates a privacy risk.
feedback.incorrect: Some are not right yet. Link each item to a job: game events for the colours and the light sensor for dimming. Detecting speech does not require storing full recordings online.

content.prompt: The setup uses a microphone that is always on. Describe one privacy concern and one way to reduce it.
content.guidance: Write at least 200 characters. Name one privacy concern and one sensible way to reduce it, for example a mute button or processing sound only on the device. Paste is disabled.

metadata.title: Scenario: a warehouse robot
metadata.summary: Identify which part of a warehouse robot's work is AI-enabled.

content.text: Scenario: a warehouse robot

An online shop uses robots in its warehouse. Each robot drives to a shelf, uses a camera to recognise the correct item, picks it up with a gripper and carries it to a packing station. It slows down if a worker walks in front of it.
Sensors (camera and distance sensor) provide the inputs. The controller processes the data. Actuators (gripper and wheels) carry out the actions.

content.prompt: Which part of the warehouse robot's work is AI-enabled rather than simple programmed movement?

options.label: Recognising the correct item from camera images
Driving forward when told to
Opening and closing the gripper
Stopping when its battery is empty

feedback.correct: Correct. Recognising items from camera images needs pattern recognition, which is AI. Driving, gripping and stopping can all be simple programmed actions.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Driving, gripping and stopping on low battery can all be programmed with fixed rules. Recognising the correct item from images needs AI pattern recognition.

metadata.title: Scenario: spotting prohibited objects
metadata.summary: Apply image recognition to screening bags for prohibited objects, including benefits and limitations.

content.text: Scenario: spotting prohibited objects

A concert venue scans bags with an X-ray machine. An image recognition system checks each scan and flags any bag that might contain a prohibited object, such as a knife or a glass bottle. Security staff then check every flagged bag by hand.

content.prompt: What is the input to the image recognition system?

options.label: The X-ray image of each bag
The warning on screen that a bag might contain a knife
The security guard's decision after checking the bag
The list of prohibited items printed at the entrance

feedback.correct: Correct. The X-ray image goes in (input). The warning on screen is the output, and the guard's check happens afterwards.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. The input is what goes into the system: the X-ray image of each bag. The on-screen warning is the output, and the guard's decision comes after the system has finished.

content.prompt: Why must the system be trained on thousands of scans showing prohibited objects in many different positions?

options.label: So that it can recognise objects even when they are turned, hidden or partly covered
So that it runs without electricity
So that it never needs updating
So that it can read the owner's name

feedback.correct: Correct. Varied training examples help the system recognise objects from different angles and positions, instead of only the exact examples it has seen.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Training data is about accuracy. The system needs many varied examples so it can still recognise a knife or bottle when it is turned, hidden or partly covered.

content.prompt: Give one benefit and one limitation of using image recognition to screen bags at the venue.
content.guidance: Write at least 200 characters. Give one benefit, such as speed or consistency, and one limitation, such as errors, bias or cost. Explain each briefly. Paste is disabled.

metadata.title: Mixed knowledge check
metadata.summary: Apply everything from Week 4 to new situations.

content.text: Mixed knowledge check
These questions mix ideas from the whole week. Read each situation carefully and use the ideas from earlier activities.

content.prompt: A school's online booking form checks that every email address contains an @ symbol before it is accepted. Is this AI?

options.label: Yes, because it checks data automatically
No, it follows one fixed rule written by a programmer
Yes, because it runs online
Yes, because it uses the cloud

feedback.correct: Correct. Checking for an @ symbol is a single fixed rule. Being automatic or online does not make software AI.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Working automatically, online or in the cloud does not make software AI. Checking for an @ symbol is one fixed rule, so it is rule-based.

content.prompt: A smart doorbell notices movement, records a short clip, recognises that the visitor is a delivery driver and sends you a notification. Which part is the processing step?

options.label: Noticing the movement
Recording the clip
Recognising that the visitor is a delivery driver
Sending the notification

feedback.correct: Correct. Recognising who is at the door is the processing step, and it uses AI image recognition. Movement is sensed, the clip is data, and the notification is the action.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Follow the flow: noticing movement is the sensor, the clip is the data, and the notification is the action. Recognising the visitor is the processing step.

content.prompt: A hospital uses a robot that follows lines on the floor to carry medicines between wards. It stops when its bump sensor is pressed. Which best describes it?

options.label: A robot using programmed behaviour, not AI
AI software with no robot body
A neural network
A DaaS service

feedback.correct: Correct. It has sensors and actuators, so it is a robot, but following lines and stopping on a bump are fixed rules. It does not need AI.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. It is a physical machine with sensors and actuators, so it is a robot. Following lines and stopping when bumped are fixed rules, so it uses programmed behaviour rather than AI.

content.prompt: A company wants a neural network to spot fraudulent card payments. What does it need first?

options.label: Lots of past payment records, each labelled as fraudulent or genuine
One fixed rule, such as "block every payment over £100"
A robot to watch the bank's cash machines
Only customers' names and home addresses

feedback.correct: Correct. A neural network learns from labelled examples. Past payments marked as fraudulent or genuine let it learn the patterns of fraud.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. A single fixed rule would be rule-based, not a neural network, and names or addresses alone show no payment patterns. A neural network learns from labelled examples: many past payments marked as fraudulent or genuine.

content.prompt: Fridge 1 sends a photo of its shelves to your phone when you ask. Fridge 2 also recognises which foods are running low and adds them to your shopping list. Which statement is correct?

options.label: Both fridges use AI because they are both connected to the internet
Fridge 1 is IoT only; Fridge 2 is IoT and AI working together
Neither fridge is IoT because fridges are not computers
Fridge 1 uses AI because it takes a photo

feedback.correct: Correct. Both are IoT because they connect and share data. Only Fridge 2 recognises what is in the photo and makes a decision, so only Fridge 2 adds AI.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Being connected makes a device IoT, not AI, and taking a photo is just sensing. Fridge 2 recognises the foods in the image and acts on it, which is where the AI comes in.

metadata.title: Extension: AI technology profile
metadata.summary: Write a short profile of one AI-enabled device or system.

content.text: Extension: AI technology profile
Optional homework or research: build a short profile you could reuse when outlining technologies for AC1.1 practice. This is formative, not Gateway assignment evidence.

content.prompt: Choose one AI-enabled device or system, such as a smart speaker, robot vacuum, self-driving car or recommendation system. Explain what it does, what data or sensors it uses, what the AI part does, one benefit and one limitation.
content.guidance: Cover what it does, the data or sensors, what the AI does, one benefit and one limitation. Write at least 500 characters. Paste is disabled.

metadata.title: Exit ticket
metadata.summary: Quick check that you can outline AI, smart devices, robots and neural networks, and rate your confidence.

content.text: Exit ticket

content.prompt: Which statement is correct?

options.label: Every robot uses AI
Every program is AI
A robot can follow programmed steps without AI, and AI can run with no robot body
Neural networks think exactly like humans

feedback.correct: Correct. Robotics and AI are different things that can work together. Many robots follow fixed programs, and much AI is software only.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Not every robot or program uses AI, and neural networks do not think like humans. Robots can run without AI, and AI can run without a robot body.

content.text: Before you finish, tell your tutor how confident you feel outlining AI, smart devices, robots and neural networks.

metadata.title: Welcome to Week 5
metadata.summary: Recap Week 4 AI ideas, then set the focus for VR, AR, 3D printing and 4D printing (AC1.1).

content.text: Welcome to Week 5
This week you outline four more emerging technologies: virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), 3D printing and 4D printing (AC1.1).

content.title: By the end of this week
content.text: You will be able to say what VR and AR are and how they differ. You will outline how 3D printing builds objects in layers. You will explain how 4D printing adds change over time. You will pick a suitable technology for simple Pixel Forge Games scenarios.
First, a quick check from Week 4. AI means software that learns from data, recognises patterns or makes predictions. Not every automatic program is AI.

content.prompt: Which statement from Week 4 is correct?

options.label: Every program that runs on a computer is AI
AI can recognise patterns or learn from data, but it does not think or feel like a person
A calculator is AI because it works quickly
Robots and AI are always the same thing

feedback.correct: Correct. AI handles tasks that usually need human intelligence, such as spotting patterns. It does not think or feel like a person, and not every program or robot is AI.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Not every program is AI, and a calculator usually follows fixed rules. Robots and AI can work together but they are not always the same thing.

content.prompt: Which four technologies will you outline this week for AC1.1?

options.label: Email, spreadsheets, passwords and printers only
Virtual reality, augmented reality, 3D printing and 4D printing
Only robots and RFID tags
Only cloud storage and Wi-Fi routers

feedback.correct: Correct. This week focuses on VR, AR, 3D printing and 4D printing so you can outline them for AC1.1.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Read the welcome text again. This week is about VR, AR, 3D printing and 4D printing.

metadata.title: Recap: smart systems and AI
metadata.summary: Refresh the smart-system flow and the difference between fixed rules and AI.

content.text: Recap: smart systems and AI
A smart system often follows Sensors, Data, Processing, then Decision or action. AI is involved when the processing learns from data or recognises patterns, not when it only follows one fixed rule.

content.prompt: Sort each example as Fixed rules or AI-style processing.

items.text: A light turns off after ten minutes with no movement
A phone groups photos by recognising faces
A music app builds a playlist from your listening habits
A microwave runs for the number of seconds you typed

feedback.correct: Well sorted. Timers and simple on/off rules are fixed. Face grouping and playlists recognise patterns or learn from data.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite yet. Ask whether the system only follows a set instruction, or whether it learns from data or recognises patterns.

metadata.title: Recap: linking earlier technologies
metadata.summary: Connect IoT, cloud and AI ideas to this week's immersive and making technologies.

content.text: Linking earlier technologies

VR, AR and 3D printing often use ideas you have already met. A headset can be a connected device (IoT). Heavy graphics or AI features can run in the cloud. Sensors on a headset track where you look and move.
You do not need to invent new words here. Use the ones you know: sensors collect data, processing makes sense of it, and an action or display updates what you see.

content.prompt: A VR headset tracks head movement and updates the scene. Which earlier idea does the tracking mainly use?

options.label: Sensors collecting data about movement
DaaS giving you a full remote desktop
RFID tags stuck on every wall
A calculator following only fixed sums

feedback.correct: Correct. Tracking uses sensors to collect movement data so the system can update what you see.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Head tracking is about sensors and data. It is not a remote desktop (DaaS), RFID on walls, or a simple calculator sum.

content.prompt: Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: VR, AR and 3D printing replace the need for any earlier digital technologies
VR, AR and 3D printing can use sensors, cloud services and software ideas you already know
Cloud computing only works with email
IoT devices can never be used with VR or AR

feedback.correct: Correct. These technologies build on sensors, networks, cloud services and software rather than replacing earlier digital tools.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. New technologies usually combine earlier ideas. Cloud is not limited to email, and connected devices can support VR or AR.

metadata.title: What is virtual reality?
metadata.summary: Define VR in simple language and give a familiar example.

content.text: What is virtual reality?
Virtual reality (VR) puts you inside a computer-made world. You usually wear a headset over your eyes. When you turn your head, the view changes as if you were really there.
The word virtual means created by software, not built from bricks or wood. The world can look like a game level, a training room or a quiet beach.
A familiar example is a VR game where you stand in a virtual arena and look around. Another example is a training simulation where a learner practises a task in a safe virtual space.

content.title: Key term: immersive
content.text: Immersive means the experience surrounds you so strongly that it feels as if you are inside it. VR aims to be immersive by filling your view and responding to your movement.

content.prompt: Which statement best defines virtual reality?

options.label: Any video watched on a phone screen
A computer-made world that surrounds you, usually through a headset
A printed poster stuck over a real object
A spreadsheet stored in the cloud

feedback.correct: Correct. VR is a computer-made world that surrounds you. A headset is the usual way to enter that world.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Watching a normal video or using a spreadsheet is not VR. VR surrounds you in a computer-made world, usually with a headset.

content.prompt: Why does turning your head matter in VR?

options.label: It charges the headset battery
The view should update so the virtual world stays lined up with your movement
It prints a 3D object
It switches the headset into a calculator

feedback.correct: Correct. Tracking your head lets the system update the view so the virtual world feels consistent as you look around.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Head movement is tracked so the display updates. It does not print objects or turn the headset into a calculator.

metadata.title: VR equipment and tracking
metadata.summary: Name common VR kit and explain what tracking does.

content.text: VR equipment and tracking
Common VR kit includes a headset (the display over your eyes), controllers (hand devices for pointing or grabbing), and sensors or cameras that track movement.
Tracking means the system keeps checking where your head and hands are. Without tracking, the virtual world would not stay lined up with how you move.
Some headsets need a powerful computer nearby. Others are standalone: the computing happens inside the headset. Both types still create a virtual world.

content.prompt: What is the main job of VR tracking?

options.label: To print plastic parts
To keep the virtual view lined up with the user's head and hand movement
To send emails automatically
To store paper documents

feedback.correct: Correct. Tracking follows movement so the virtual view stays lined up with the user.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Tracking is about movement and the display. Printing, email and paper storage are different jobs.

content.prompt: A learner puts on a headset and holds two hand controllers. Which statement is correct?

options.label: Only the headset matters; controllers are never used in VR
The headset shows the world; controllers can let the learner point, grab or select in that world
Controllers replace the need for any display
Tracking only works if the room has no light

feedback.correct: Correct. The headset is the display. Controllers are common tools for interacting inside the virtual world.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Controllers support interaction. They do not replace the display, and tracking does not require a pitch-dark room.

metadata.title: Where VR is used
metadata.summary: Outline practical VR applications beyond entertainment.

content.text: Where VR is used
VR is well known for games, but it is also used for training, design reviews and virtual visits. For example, a trainee can practise a safety drill without real danger.
Designers can walk through a virtual building before it is built. Museums and schools can offer virtual tours of places that are hard to visit.
These uses are already happening in many organisations. They are practical applications, not science fiction.

content.prompt: Which is a practical use of VR outside entertainment?

options.label: Training someone in a safe virtual environment before they try the real task
Editing a spreadsheet with no display
Sending a text message with no graphics
Printing a paper poster with no headset

feedback.correct: Correct. Safe training simulations are a real and useful VR application.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. VR can support training and virtual visits. Spreadsheets, plain texts and paper posters alone are not VR uses.

content.prompt: A design team wants to check how a new shop layout feels before building it. How can VR help?

options.label: By letting the team walk through a virtual version of the shop
By replacing the design drawings with a paper calculator
By turning the shop plan into an email attachment only
By hiding the design so nobody can review it

feedback.correct: Correct. A virtual walkthrough lets people review a design before expensive building work begins.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. VR helps people experience a design digitally so they can review it before building.

metadata.title: VR or not VR?
metadata.summary: Classify examples as VR or not VR using the surround-and-headset idea.

content.text: VR or not VR?
Ask: does the person enter a computer-made world that surrounds their view, usually with a headset? Looking at a normal flat screen in the real room is not the same as VR.

content.prompt: For each example, choose VR or Not VR.

items.text: A learner wears a headset and stands inside a virtual training kitchen
A student watches a normal YouTube video on a laptop screen
A gamer looks around a fully virtual arena using a headset
A tourist reads a paper map on a street corner

feedback.correct: Well sorted. Headset experiences that surround you are VR. A laptop video or paper map stays in the real world as a flat view.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. VR surrounds you in a computer-made world, usually with a headset. A normal laptop video or paper map is not VR.

metadata.title: VR benefits and limitations
metadata.summary: Weigh up benefits and limitations of VR for learners and organisations.

content.text: VR benefits and limitations
Benefits of VR include safe practice, strong immersion and the chance to visit places that are hard to reach. Teams can also review designs together in a shared virtual space.
Limitations include cost of headsets, the need for space to move safely, motion sickness for some users, and the time needed to build good virtual content.
VR can be useful, but it is not the right tool for every job. Sometimes a simple video or a real practice session is clearer and cheaper.

content.prompt: Which statement is a limitation of VR?

options.label: It can let people practise dangerous tasks safely
Some users feel motion sickness and headsets can be expensive
It can support immersive games
It can show a virtual building before it is built

feedback.correct: Correct. Cost and motion sickness are real limitations. The other options are benefits or uses.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Safe practice, immersion and virtual walkthroughs are benefits. Cost and sickness risk are limitations.

content.prompt: In two or three sentences, give one benefit and one limitation of using VR for training.
content.guidance: Sentence starters: One benefit of VR for training is... One limitation is... Write at least 200 characters.

metadata.title: What is augmented reality?
metadata.summary: Define AR and contrast it with replacing the real world.

content.text: What is augmented reality?
Augmented reality (AR) adds digital objects on top of the real world. You still see your room, street or classroom. Extra labels, characters or arrows appear over what the camera sees.
Augmented means added to. AR does not usually replace the whole view with a virtual world. It layers helpful digital information onto reality.
A familiar example is a phone app that places a virtual character on your living-room floor through the camera. Another example is an app that shows directions as arrows over the street view.

content.title: Note
content.text: VR surrounds you in a virtual world. AR keeps the real world and adds digital extras on top.

content.prompt: Which statement best defines augmented reality?

options.label: A headset that blocks out the real world completely
Digital information or objects added on top of the real world
A printer that builds plastic layers
A cloud folder used only for spreadsheets

feedback.correct: Correct. AR adds digital content to what you already see in the real world.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Blocking out the real world is closer to VR. Printing layers is 3D printing. AR adds digital extras to reality.

content.prompt: A learner points a phone camera at a desk and a virtual game character appears on the desk. Which technology is this?

options.label: VR, because the desk disappears
AR, because the real desk stays visible and a digital object is added
4D printing, because the character is plastic
RFID, because the phone scanned a paper tag

feedback.correct: Correct. The real desk remains visible while a digital character is added. That is AR.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. If the real scene stays and digital objects are layered on top, it is AR, not VR or printing.

metadata.title: Devices used for AR
metadata.summary: Identify phones, tablets and AR glasses as common AR devices.

content.text: Devices used for AR
Most school and everyday AR uses a smartphone or tablet camera. The screen shows the real scene plus digital overlays.
Some workplaces use AR glasses. These leave your hands free while labels or instructions appear in front of you.
You do not always need an expensive headset for AR. Many useful AR tools already run on devices learners know.

content.prompt: Which device is commonly used for everyday AR?

options.label: A smartphone or tablet camera and screen
A paper notebook with no camera
A toaster with no display
A wired keyboard with no internet and no camera

feedback.correct: Correct. Phones and tablets are the most common everyday AR devices.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. AR needs a camera view of the real world and a way to show digital overlays. Phones and tablets do that well.

content.prompt: Why might a technician prefer AR glasses instead of holding a phone?

options.label: Glasses always print plastic parts
Hands-free overlays can show instructions while both hands stay on the job
Glasses remove the need for any training
Phones cannot show any digital information

feedback.correct: Correct. AR glasses can keep instructions visible while hands stay free for the task.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. The advantage is hands-free guidance. Glasses do not print parts or replace all training, and phones can also show digital information.

metadata.title: Where AR is used
metadata.summary: Outline AR uses in learning, navigation and product preview.

content.text: Where AR is used
AR can label parts of a machine for training, show furniture in your room before you buy it, or add navigation arrows over a street view.
In education, AR can place a 3D model of a heart or engine on a desk so learners can walk around it. In retail, shoppers can preview products at home.
These are current, practical uses. They help people understand something in context without building a full virtual world.

content.prompt: Which is a practical AR use?

options.label: Showing a virtual sofa in your real living room through a phone camera
Blocking out the whole room with a fully virtual beach for every task
Building a physical house with no design file and no camera
Editing a spreadsheet with the camera switched off

feedback.correct: Correct. Product preview in a real room is a common AR use.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. AR adds digital content to a real scene. Fully replacing the view is closer to VR.

content.prompt: A tutor wants learners to see labels on a real classroom 3D printer. How can AR help?

options.label: By overlaying names of parts on the live camera view of the printer
By hiding the printer completely behind a virtual wall
By removing all safety guidance from the lesson
By turning the printer into a text-only email

feedback.correct: Correct. AR can place labels on top of the real printer through a camera view.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. AR supports learning by adding clear digital labels to the real object.

metadata.title: AR or not AR?
metadata.summary: Classify examples as AR or not AR.

content.text: AR or not AR?
Ask: does the person still see the real world, with digital extras added? If the real world is fully replaced by a virtual scene, it is not AR.

content.prompt: For each example, choose AR or Not AR.

items.text: A phone shows arrows over the live street to guide you to a shop
A headset blocks the room and shows only a virtual desert
A catalogue app places a virtual lamp on your real table
A learner reads a printed textbook with no camera overlay

feedback.correct: Well sorted. Live overlays on the real world are AR. A fully virtual headset scene or a plain textbook is not AR.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. AR keeps the real world and adds digital extras. A full virtual-only view is closer to VR.

metadata.title: AR benefits and limitations
metadata.summary: Identify benefits and limitations of AR.

content.text: AR benefits and limitations
Benefits of AR include using familiar devices, keeping users aware of their real surroundings, and adding clear guidance in context.
Limitations include needing a clear camera view, possible distraction, battery use, and overlays that can be inaccurate if tracking fails.

content.prompt: Which statement is a benefit of AR compared with fully immersive VR?

options.label: Users can often keep seeing the real room or workplace while digital help is added
AR always costs more than any other technology
AR never needs a camera
AR always blocks out the real world

feedback.correct: Correct. AR usually keeps the real world visible, which can be safer and more practical for many tasks.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. A key AR benefit is seeing the real surroundings with digital extras. AR typically needs a camera view and does not block out reality.

content.prompt: Which is a limitation of AR?

options.label: It can label real objects for training
Poor lighting or tracking errors can make overlays sit in the wrong place
It can preview products at home
It can run on many smartphones

feedback.correct: Correct. If tracking fails, overlays can look wrong. The other options are benefits or strengths.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Labelling, product preview and phone support are strengths. Tracking and lighting problems are limitations.

metadata.title: VR and AR: the key difference
metadata.summary: Explain the core difference between VR and AR in plain language.

content.text: VR and AR: the key difference
VR replaces what you see with a virtual world. AR keeps the real world and adds digital extras.
Both can be interactive and both can use sensors. The deciding question is: are you inside a computer-made world, or are you still looking at the real place with extras on top?

content.prompt: What is the clearest difference between VR and AR?

options.label: VR surrounds you in a virtual world; AR adds digital content to the real world
VR only works on paper; AR only works underwater
AR always needs a full headset that blocks reality; VR never uses a display
They are identical and the names are random

feedback.correct: Correct. That surrounding-versus-overlay difference is the key idea for Level 2.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. VR surrounds you in a virtual world. AR overlays digital content on reality.

content.prompt: A museum app shows dinosaur labels over exhibits through a phone camera. Is this closer to VR or AR?

options.label: AR, because the real exhibits stay visible with digital labels added
VR, because the museum building disappears
4D printing, because labels are made of plastic
Neither, because phones cannot show digital text

feedback.correct: Correct. Real exhibits remain in view while labels are added. That is AR.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. If the real scene stays and digital labels are added, it is AR.

metadata.title: Sort benefits and limitations
metadata.summary: Classify statements as a benefit or a limitation for VR or AR.

content.text: Sort benefits and limitations
You already know the VR versus AR difference. Now sort each statement as a Benefit or a Limitation. Use what you learned about cost, safety, immersion and staying aware of real surroundings.

content.prompt: Sort each statement as Benefit or Limitation.

items.text: VR lets trainees practise risky tasks without real danger
Some VR users feel motion sickness and headsets can be expensive
AR can keep the real workplace visible while adding helpful labels
AR overlays can sit in the wrong place if tracking or lighting is poor

feedback.correct: Well sorted. Safe practice and in-context labels are benefits. Cost, sickness and tracking errors are limitations.
feedback.incorrect: Ask whether the statement helps the user or organisation, or whether it is a drawback such as cost, sickness or tracking errors.

metadata.title: Choose VR or AR for the job
metadata.summary: Select the more suitable technology for short workplace scenarios.

content.text: Choose VR or AR for the job
Read each need carefully. If people must stay aware of a real place, AR is often better. If they need a fully controlled virtual environment, VR is often better.

content.prompt: Warehouse staff need labels on real shelves while they walk the aisle. Which technology fits better?

options.label: AR overlays on a phone or glasses while the real aisle stays visible
VR that hides the warehouse completely
4D printing that turns shelves into water
A paper calculator with no display of the shelves

feedback.correct: Correct. Staff still need to see the real shelves, so AR overlays are the better fit.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Hiding the warehouse would make picking harder. They need digital help on top of the real aisle.

content.prompt: A team wants to practise evacuating a building that is still being designed and does not exist yet. Which technology fits better?

options.label: VR, so learners can enter a virtual version of the planned building
AR overlays on an empty field with no virtual building model
3D printing a single brick with no practice scenario
Cloud storage that only saves files with no building view

feedback.correct: Correct. When the real building is not there yet, a virtual world (VR) can provide a safe practice space.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Practising in a building that does not exist yet usually needs a virtual environment, which is VR.

metadata.title: What is 3D printing?
metadata.summary: Define 3D printing as building a solid object from a digital design.

content.text: What is 3D printing?
3D printing builds a solid object from a digital design. The printer usually adds material layer by layer until the shape is complete.
The digital design is often made in 3D modelling software. The printer then follows that design. Without a design file, the printer does not know what to build.
A familiar school example is printing a small plastic phone stand or a simple game-character model for a display.

content.title: Key idea
content.text: 3D printing is additive manufacturing: material is added in layers. That is different from carving material away from a block.

content.prompt: Which statement best defines 3D printing?

options.label: Building a solid object from a digital design, usually layer by layer
Taking a photo of an object
Sending an email with an attachment
Watching a flat video on a phone

feedback.correct: Correct. 3D printing turns a digital design into a physical object, usually by adding layers.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Photos, emails and videos are not 3D printing. 3D printing builds a physical object from a design.

content.prompt: Why does a 3D printer need a digital design?

options.label: So it knows the shape and size to build
So it can cook food
So it can replace the school Wi-Fi
So it can write essays automatically

feedback.correct: Correct. The design tells the printer what to make.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. The design file guides the shape. Printing does not cook food, run Wi-Fi or write essays.

metadata.title: The basic 3D printing process
metadata.summary: Order the main steps from design to finished object.

content.text: The basic 3D printing process
A simple process is: create or download a 3D design, prepare the file for the printer, print layer by layer, then finish the object (for example remove supports and check the part).

content.prompt: Put the steps in order. Use each step once.

items.text: The printer builds the object layer by layer
A digital 3D design is created or chosen
Supports are removed and the part is checked
The design is prepared as instructions the printer can follow

feedback.correct: Correct order. Design first, then prepare instructions, then print layers, then finish and check the part.
feedback.incorrect: Not in the right order yet. You need a design before the printer can be instructed. Printing happens before finishing the part.

content.prompt: What does "layer by layer" mean in 3D printing?

options.label: The printer adds thin layers of material one after another to build the shape
The printer deletes layers of a spreadsheet
The printer only prints flat posters
The printer paints an existing metal car

feedback.correct: Correct. Most school 3D printers build height by stacking thin layers of material.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Layer by layer means adding material gradually to form the 3D shape.

metadata.title: Materials and school printers
metadata.summary: Outline common materials and safe classroom expectations.

content.text: Materials and school printers
Many school printers use plastic filament that is heated and placed in layers. Other industrial printers can use resins, powders or even metal, but those systems are specialised.
Different materials suit different jobs. A display model may use a cheap plastic. A stronger part may need a tougher material and a more advanced printer.
Safety matters: hot nozzles, moving parts and fumes mean learners follow tutor rules and do not touch a printer mid-print without permission.

content.prompt: Which material is common in many school 3D printers?

options.label: Plastic filament that is heated and laid down in layers
Liquid nitrogen used as ink for paper posters
Wet cement poured into a keyboard
Cloud storage folders

feedback.correct: Correct. Heated plastic filament is common in classroom printers.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. School printers usually melt and place plastic filament. Cloud folders are not a printing material.

content.prompt: Why might an industrial metal 3D printer be unsuitable for a normal classroom?

options.label: It can need specialised equipment, training and safety controls beyond a typical school setup
Metal printing never exists anywhere
All metal printers fit in a pencil case
Metal printers only print emails

feedback.correct: Correct. Industrial metal systems are specialised. Schools usually start with safer plastic filament printers.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Metal 3D printing exists in industry, but it is not a typical classroom starter technology.

metadata.title: Applications of 3D printing
metadata.summary: Identify practical 3D printing uses including prototypes.

content.text: Applications of 3D printing
3D printing is widely used for prototypes: early versions of a product made quickly so a design can be tested and improved.
Other uses include custom tools, replacement parts, medical models for planning, and teaching aids. Some fashion and jewellery makers also print complex shapes.
3D printing is excellent for one-off or small-batch items. For millions of identical parts, traditional factory methods can still be faster and cheaper.

content.prompt: What is a prototype in this context?

options.label: An early physical version of a design made so it can be tested and improved
The final mass-produced product sold in every shop worldwide
A random file with no shape
A password for the school network

feedback.correct: Correct. Prototypes help teams test ideas before committing to expensive final production.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. A prototype is an early test version, not necessarily the final mass-produced item.

content.prompt: When is 3D printing often a good choice?

options.label: When you need a custom or small-batch part quickly from a digital design
When you need a billion identical screws at the lowest factory cost with no design changes
When you only need to send a text message
When you want to avoid having any design at all

feedback.correct: Correct. Custom and small-batch work suits 3D printing well.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Huge identical runs often suit traditional manufacturing better. Printing still needs a design.

metadata.title: 3D printing benefits and limitations
metadata.summary: Balance speed and customisation against strength, time and cost limits.

content.text: 3D printing benefits and limitations
Benefits include fast prototyping, custom shapes, less waste than some cutting methods, and the ability to make parts on demand.
Limitations include print time for large objects, limited strength of some plastics, surface finish that may need sanding, and the cost of larger industrial machines.

content.prompt: Which statement is a benefit of 3D printing?

options.label: You can turn a digital design into a custom physical prototype relatively quickly
Every printed plastic part is always stronger than steel
Printing never takes any time
You never need a design file

feedback.correct: Correct. Fast custom prototypes are a major benefit.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Strength and time depend on the job. You still need a design, and plastic is not always stronger than steel.

content.prompt: Explain one benefit and one limitation of 3D printing for a small business making prototypes.
content.guidance: Sentence starters: One benefit for a small business is... One limitation is... Write at least 200 characters.

metadata.title: What is 4D printing?
metadata.summary: Introduce 4D printing as printed objects that can change after printing.

content.text: What is 4D printing?
4D printing starts like 3D printing: an object is built from a digital design. The extra idea is that the finished object can change shape or behaviour later when conditions change.
The "fourth dimension" here means time. After printing, the object may bend, unfold or stiffen when it meets heat, water or light.
4D printing is still emerging. Some research and specialist projects already exist, but it is not as common in schools as basic 3D printing.

content.title: Be clear
content.text: Treat everyday classroom plastic prints as 3D printing unless the material is designed to change later. Do not claim every 3D print is 4D.

content.prompt: What extra idea does 4D printing add to 3D printing?

options.label: The printed object can change shape or behaviour over time when conditions change
The printer only prints in black and white
The object can never be touched
The design file is deleted automatically

feedback.correct: Correct. Time and change after printing are the key 4D idea.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. 4D printing is about designed change after printing, not about deleting files or forbidding touch.

content.prompt: Which statement is most accurate for Level 2 learners?

options.label: 4D printing is an emerging idea; some specialist examples exist, but school work usually starts with 3D printing
Every home already uses 4D printers for toast
4D printing replaced all factories in 1990
4D printing means drawing on paper with four pencils

feedback.correct: Correct. Keep 4D printing in the emerging-technology category while recognising real research and specialist uses.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. 4D printing is emerging and specialist. Everyday school making usually starts with 3D printing.

metadata.title: How 4D printing differs from 3D printing
metadata.summary: Compare 3D and 4D printing with clear examples.

content.text: How 4D printing differs from 3D printing
A normal 3D-printed phone stand keeps its shape after printing. That is 3D printing.
A 4D-printed object is made so that a later trigger, such as heat or water, causes a planned change. The change is designed, not an accident.

content.prompt: A plastic keyring is printed and stays the same shape on a learner's bag. What is this?

options.label: 3D printing of a stable object
4D printing, because time always turns every object into 4D
VR, because the keyring is virtual
AR, because the keyring is a label

feedback.correct: Correct. A finished object that is meant to stay the same is a normal 3D print.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Time passing alone does not make something 4D. 4D needs a designed change after printing.

content.prompt: Which example is closer to 4D printing?

options.label: A printed strip designed to curl when placed in warm water
A printed cube that is sanded smooth and then left unchanged
A photo of a cube on a phone
A cloud backup of a spreadsheet

feedback.correct: Correct. A planned response to a trigger such as warm water matches the 4D idea.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Sanding a stable cube is finishing a 3D print. Photos and spreadsheets are not 4D printing.

metadata.title: Triggers that can change a 4D object
metadata.summary: Identify heat, water and light as example triggers.

content.text: Triggers that can change a 4D object
Researchers often design materials that react to heat, water or light. The trigger is chosen to match the job. Not every material reacts to every trigger.

content.prompt: Sort each item as a possible 4D trigger example or Not a trigger example.

items.text: Warm water that makes a printed strip curl
Heat that causes a designed fold to open
A random password with no effect on the material
Light that changes a specially designed material

feedback.correct: Well sorted. Heat, water and light can be designed triggers. A password does not change the material by itself.
feedback.incorrect: Look for conditions that act on the material, such as heat, water or light. A password is not a physical trigger.

content.prompt: Why must a 4D trigger be planned in the design?

options.label: So the change is controlled and useful, not a surprise failure
So the printer can send emails
So the object never needs a design file
So VR headsets become unnecessary forever

feedback.correct: Correct. 4D printing is about designed change, not accidental melting or breaking.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. The point of a trigger is a planned, useful response built into the design.

metadata.title: 4D printing: practical today and possible later
metadata.summary: Separate current specialist uses from speculative future ideas.

content.text: Practical today and possible later
Today, 4D printing appears mainly in research labs and specialist projects. Examples include experimental medical devices and adaptive structures.
Possible future ideas include packaging that changes shape in transit, or adaptive sports equipment. These ideas need careful testing before everyday use.
