For AC1.1, you should be able to outline the idea and give a sensible example. You should also say clearly when something is still experimental.

content.prompt: Which statement is fairest about 4D printing today?

options.label: It is an emerging technology with specialist and research examples, not a common school printer feature
Every supermarket already sells home 4D printers for toast
4D printing is imaginary and has never been researched
4D printing is identical to watching VR videos

feedback.correct: Correct. Keep your answer balanced: emerging and specialist, not everyday classroom kit.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. 4D printing is researched and specialist, but it is not everyday school equipment or the same as VR.

content.prompt: A learner claims a 4D object will change usefully with no designed material and no trigger. What is wrong?

options.label: The claim is speculative and ignores how designs, materials and triggers actually work
Nothing is wrong because every printed object is automatically 4D
4D printing never needs a digital design
4D printing is the same as watching a flat video

feedback.correct: Correct. Good Level 2 answers stay realistic. Designed material change needs a plan and a trigger.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Outline real ideas carefully. Do not invent change with no design or trigger.

metadata.title: Pixel Forge Games: VR and AR choices
metadata.summary: Apply VR and AR to Pixel Forge Games product ideas.

content.text: Pixel Forge Games: VR and AR choices

Pixel Forge Games is a fictional games development company used across this course. The studio designs digital games and is now exploring emerging technologies that could improve how players experience those games.

This week the design team is comparing two ideas. Idea A is a headset game where players feel fully inside a fantasy arena. Idea B is a phone game where digital creatures appear on real pavements through the camera.
Both ideas can be valuable. The team must match the technology to the player experience they want.

content.prompt: Pixel Forge wants players to feel fully inside a fantasy arena. Which technology fits best?

options.label: VR with a headset so the player is surrounded by the virtual arena
AR labels on a paper instruction sheet only
3D printing a single plastic coin for the desk
A spreadsheet of enemy names with no graphics

feedback.correct: Correct. Feeling fully inside an arena is a VR goal.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Full immersion in a virtual arena points to VR, not paper labels or a spreadsheet.

content.prompt: Pixel Forge wants a mobile game where creatures appear on real pavements through the phone camera. Which technology fits best?

options.label: AR that keeps the real street visible and adds digital creatures
VR that hides the street completely behind a headset view
3D printing that builds a pavement model with no camera view
Cloud storage that only saves files without showing the street

feedback.correct: Correct. Digital creatures on a live camera view of real streets is AR.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. If the real street stays visible with digital extras, choose AR.

metadata.title: Pixel Forge Games: 3D and 4D making
metadata.summary: Use 3D printing for prototypes and keep 4D ideas clearly experimental.

content.text: Pixel Forge Games: 3D and 4D making
Pixel Forge Games is the same fictional studio. Alongside digital games, its hardware team sometimes makes physical objects to test how controllers feel and to show characters on marketing desks.
Today the team needs a prototype controller grip and a small character model. Those jobs suit everyday 3D printing from a digital design.

A researcher also suggests an experimental accessory that changes stiffness when warmed by a player's hand. That idea would need specialist 4D materials and careful testing. It is not a normal school print.

content.prompt: Which job is a clear, practical use of 3D printing for Pixel Forge today?

options.label: Printing a prototype controller grip from a digital design so the shape can be tested
Printing a finished million-unit factory run with no design review
Replacing all game software with plastic parts
Using a headset to hide the real workshop completely

feedback.correct: Correct. Prototyping a grip is a realistic 3D printing use.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Prototypes and models are practical now. Huge unreviewed factory runs are not a sensible first step.

content.prompt: How should the team describe the hand-warming accessory idea?

options.label: As an experimental 4D-style concept that would need specialist materials and testing
As a standard school 3D print that every learner already makes each lesson
As proof that 4D printing is identical to AR
As a finished product already sold worldwide with no risks

feedback.correct: Correct. Keep speculative adaptive materials in the experimental category.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Adaptive change after printing is closer to emerging 4D ideas and needs careful testing.

metadata.title: Pixel Forge Games: pick the right technology
metadata.summary: Select suitable technologies for mixed Pixel Forge scenarios.

content.text: Pixel Forge Games: pick the right technology

Pixel Forge Games is deciding which emerging technology fits each job. Use the ideas from this week: VR for fully virtual worlds, AR for digital extras on the real world, 3D printing for stable physical prototypes, and 4D printing only for experimental designed change after printing.
Match each need to the best technology. Prefer practical options first. Mark futuristic ideas as experimental when needed.

content.prompt: Match each Pixel Forge need to the best technology.

items.text: Playtest a headset game set entirely inside a virtual spaceship
Let fans point a phone at a poster so a character appears on top of it
Make a quick plastic prototype of a new controller shape
Research a material that softens when warmed by the player's hand

feedback.correct: Well matched. Virtual-only play is VR, poster overlays are AR, prototypes are 3D printing, and adaptive materials are experimental 4D ideas.
feedback.incorrect: Try again. Ask whether the world is fully virtual, overlaid on reality, a stable printed object, or a designed change after printing.

metadata.title: Knowledge check: VR, AR and printing
metadata.summary: Check key AC1.1 ideas from this week without repeating earlier wording.

content.text: Knowledge check

content.prompt: A training company wants staff to practise a dangerous drill before using real equipment. Which technology is the best fit?

options.label: VR, so staff can practise inside a safe virtual environment
AR labels on a blank wall with no practise scenario
3D printing a poster with no interactive practice
4D printing with no designed training task

feedback.correct: Correct. Safe practice of a dangerous drill is a strong VR use.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. When people need a controlled practice world, VR is usually the better fit.

content.prompt: A warehouse needs digital shelf labels while staff still see the real aisle. Which technology is the best fit?

options.label: AR overlays that keep the real aisle visible
VR that hides the warehouse completely
3D printing that replaces every shelf overnight
4D printing with no warehouse task

feedback.correct: Correct. Staff still need the real aisle, so AR overlays are the better fit.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Keeping the real workplace visible with digital help points to AR.

content.prompt: Which statement about 3D printing is correct?

options.label: It builds a physical object from a digital design, often layer by layer
It only edits cloud spreadsheets
It always creates food from light alone
It means watching a flat video

feedback.correct: Correct. Design to physical object, usually in layers, is the core 3D printing idea.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. 3D printing makes physical objects from designs.

content.prompt: How does 4D printing differ from ordinary 3D printing?

options.label: The object is designed to change later when conditions such as heat or water change
The object can never leave the computer screen
The printer refuses to use any digital design
It is another name for AR glasses

feedback.correct: Correct. Designed change after printing is the 4D difference.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. 4D printing still starts with a physical printed object, then adds planned change over time.

content.prompt: Pixel Forge needs a plastic desk model of a character for a marketing stand. Which technology is the most practical first choice?

options.label: 3D printing a prototype model from a digital design
4D printing that must change shape every minute to be useful on a desk
VR that only exists inside a headset
AR overlays with no physical model at all

feedback.correct: Correct. A stable physical marketing model is a classic 3D printing job.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. A desk model needs a physical object. Start with 3D printing.

metadata.title: Knowledge check: benefits, limits and choices
metadata.summary: Apply benefits, limitations and technology choice to short cases.

content.text: Knowledge check: benefits, limits and choices

content.prompt: Which pair correctly matches a benefit to a limitation?

options.label: VR can support safe training; VR headsets can be costly and some users feel sick
AR never needs a camera; AR always blocks the real world
3D printing never needs a design; 3D printing always makes steel stronger than titanium
4D printing is identical to email; email is identical to VR

feedback.correct: Correct. Safe training is a VR benefit; cost and sickness risk are limitations.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Look for a true benefit paired with a true limitation.

content.prompt: Staff must keep both hands on a real machine while seeing step labels. Which choice is best?

options.label: AR glasses or a carefully placed AR display that keeps the real machine visible
VR that hides the machine completely
3D printing a new machine during the repair
Removing all step labels from the job

feedback.correct: Correct. Hands-free guidance on a real machine points to AR.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Hiding the machine would make the job harder. They need overlays on reality.

content.prompt: Why might a business still use factory moulds instead of 3D printing for a million identical parts?

options.label: Traditional methods can be faster and cheaper for very large identical runs
3D printing cannot make any physical object
Factories are not allowed to use digital designs
Million-part runs never need quality checks

feedback.correct: Correct. 3D printing suits custom and small batches. Huge identical runs often suit other methods.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Scale and cost matter. 3D printing helps with custom work, but it is not always best for huge identical runs.

content.prompt: Which statement shows good Level 2 judgement about 4D printing?

options.label: It is emerging; outline the idea and keep speculative products clearly experimental
It already replaced all packaging worldwide last year
It means the same as watching a tutorial video
It only exists as a spelling mistake for 3D printing

feedback.correct: Correct. Balanced answers outline the idea without over-claiming.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Treat 4D printing as emerging and specialist, not as science fiction or a typo.

metadata.title: Extension: technology profile homework
metadata.summary: Optional homework: build a short AC1.1-style profile of one Week 5 technology.

content.text: Extension: technology profile homework

Optional homework or research: choose VR, AR, 3D printing or 4D printing and write a short profile you could reuse when outlining technologies for AC1.1 practice. This is formative, not Gateway assignment evidence.

content.prompt: Choose one technology from this week (VR, AR, 3D printing or 4D printing). Explain what it is, give one practical example, one benefit, one limitation, and say whether your example is everyday, specialist or experimental.
content.guidance: Sentence starters: The technology I chose is... It means... One practical example is... One benefit is... One limitation is... My example is everyday / specialist / experimental because... Write at least 500 characters. Paste is disabled.

metadata.title: Exit ticket
metadata.summary: Quick check that you can outline VR, AR, 3D printing and 4D printing, and rate your confidence.

content.text: Exit ticket

content.prompt: Which short summary is correct?

options.label: VR surrounds you; AR adds digital extras to the real world; 3D prints objects; 4D adds planned change later
VR, AR, 3D printing and 4D printing are four names for the same phone app
3D printing means watching videos and VR means printing plastic
AR always hides the real world completely

feedback.correct: Correct. That short summary captures the four ideas from this week.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Keep the four ideas separate: surround (VR), overlay (AR), build objects (3D), planned change later (4D).

content.text: Before you finish, tell your tutor how confident you feel outlining VR, AR, 3D printing and 4D printing.

metadata.title: Welcome to Week 6
metadata.summary: Recap Week 5 ideas, then set the focus for 5G, IPv6, blockchain, serverless computing and SD-WAN (AC1.1).

content.text: Welcome to Week 6

This week you outline five more emerging technologies: 5G (fifth-generation mobile networks), IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6), blockchain, serverless computing and SD-WAN (Software-Defined Wide Area Network) (AC1.1).

content.title: By the end of this week
content.text: You will be able to describe what each technology is, give a practical use for each one, and explain how they differ. You will use Pixel Forge Games examples where they help you see real workplace uses.

First, a quick check from Week 5. Virtual reality (VR) surrounds you in a computer-made world. Augmented reality (AR) adds digital extras to the real world. 3D printing builds objects in layers. 4D printing adds planned change over time.

content.prompt: Which statement from Week 5 is correct?

options.label: VR and AR are two names for the same flat phone video

metadata.title: Linking earlier technologies
metadata.summary: Connect IoT, cloud and networks to this week's infrastructure technologies.

content.text: Linking earlier technologies
You have already met connected devices (the Internet of Things, or IoT), cloud services and wireless ideas. This week's technologies often support those systems behind the scenes.

5G can carry mobile traffic for games and devices. IPv6 helps give more devices their own network addresses. Blockchain can record histories of digital items. Serverless computing can run small pieces of cloud code. SD-WAN can link company sites together.

content.prompt: Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: This week's technologies replace everything you learned in Weeks 1 to 5
This week's technologies often support networks, devices and cloud services you already know
Cloud computing only works with paper forms
IoT devices never need network addresses

feedback.correct: Correct. New technologies usually build on networks, devices and cloud services rather than wiping them out.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Think of this week as adding tools that help networks and applications work at scale.

content.prompt: Pixel Forge Games wants smoother mobile play, more connected devices and linked offices. Why does that fit this week?

options.label: Because the topics cover mobile networks, IP addressing, cloud code and site-to-site networking
Because the only topic this week is 3D printing plastic cases
Because games never use networks
Because AC1.1 only covers paper-based technologies

feedback.correct: Correct. Mobile networks, addressing, cloud functions and wide-area links all appear in this week's five technologies.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Pixel Forge's needs map to the networking and cloud ideas in this week's list.

metadata.title: What is 5G?
metadata.summary: Define 5G as fifth-generation mobile network technology in plain English.

content.text: What is 5G?

5G means fifth-generation mobile network technology. It is the next major step after earlier mobile generations such as 4G. Phones, tablets and some connected devices can use 5G where coverage is available.
In suitable conditions, 5G can provide high-speed mobile connectivity. It can also support many connected devices in the same area. That matters for busy cities, stadiums and large events.

content.title: Key idea
content.text: 5G is about mobile networks. It is not a new games console, and it is not the same thing as home Wi-Fi, even though both can give wireless internet access.

content.prompt: What does 5G stand for in this unit?

options.label: Fifth-generation mobile network technology
Five free games online
A type of 3D printer filament
A blockchain wallet password

feedback.correct: Correct. 5G means fifth-generation mobile network technology.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Expand the acronym: fifth-generation mobile network technology.

content.prompt: Which statement about 5G is most accurate?

options.label: It can support high-speed mobile connections and many devices where the network is ready
It always works at full speed in every building worldwide
It only works on paper maps
It replaces the need for any IP addresses

feedback.correct: Correct. 5G can offer high speed and support many devices, but only where the network and conditions allow it.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Coverage and conditions still matter. 5G does not remove the need for IP addressing.

metadata.title: What does latency mean?
metadata.summary: Explain latency with a simple gaming example and link it to 5G claims.

content.text: What does latency mean?
Latency is the delay before a response arrives. In a game, high latency can mean you press jump and the character jumps a moment later. Low latency means the response feels quicker.
5G can offer lower latency in suitable conditions. That can help cloud games, live mobile apps and some connected-device control. It does not guarantee perfect response times everywhere.

content.title: Simple example
content.text: Think about sending a message from your phone to a game server. Latency is the wait before the server's reply reaches you. Shorter waits feel more responsive.

content.prompt: What does latency mean?

options.label: The delay before a response arrives
The colour of a headset cable
The number of 3D printer layers
The title of a spreadsheet

feedback.correct: Correct. Latency is delay. Lower latency usually feels more responsive.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Latency is about waiting time for a response, not colour, printing or document titles.

content.prompt: A Pixel Forge Games player taps fire on a mobile match. Which situation shows lower latency?

options.label: The shot appears almost straight away
The shot appears several seconds later every time
The phone refuses to connect to any network
The game deletes the player's account

feedback.correct: Correct. A quick on-screen response is what lower latency feels like to a player.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Lower latency means less waiting between action and response.

metadata.title: Where 5G can be used
metadata.summary: Outline practical 5G uses in gaming, apps, devices and other industries.

content.text: Where 5G can be used
Possible uses include mobile gaming with smoother downloads and play, apps that need quick responses, and connected devices that share data while people move around.
Other industries can use 5G too. Examples include venues with thousands of phones online at once, remote support for technicians, and vehicles or sensors that need mobile connectivity.
At Pixel Forge Games, a demo team might stream a build preview to phones at a show, or test multiplayer play over a busy mobile network.

content.prompt: Which is a practical use of 5G?

options.label: Supporting many phones and devices with high-speed mobile connectivity at a busy event
Printing plastic figures without any network
Writing on paper with no digital devices
Turning off all mobile networks forever

feedback.correct: Correct. Busy events and mobile applications are realistic places where 5G can help.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Look for a mobile-network use, not an offline paper or printing task.

content.prompt: Why might a mobile game benefit from 5G in suitable conditions?

options.label: Faster downloads and more responsive play can improve the player experience
5G deletes the need for game design
5G always removes every in-game delay worldwide
5G means the game must be played on paper

feedback.correct: Correct. Speed and responsiveness can help mobile games when coverage and conditions are good.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. 5G can improve mobile experiences, but it does not replace design or guarantee perfect play everywhere.

metadata.title: Why 5G performance still varies
metadata.summary: Explain that coverage, congestion, devices and services affect 5G results.

content.text: Why 5G performance still varies
5G performance still depends on coverage (whether a 5G signal is available), network congestion (how busy the network is), the device being used, and the service the person is trying to reach.
A phone can show a 5G icon and still feel slow if the mast is busy, the building blocks the signal, or the game server is overloaded. Marketing claims are not the same as every real-world result.

content.prompt: Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: 5G performance depends on coverage, congestion, devices and the service being used
Any phone with a 5G label always gets the same top speed everywhere
Buildings never affect mobile signals
Game servers never cause delay

feedback.correct: Correct. Real performance depends on several factors, not only the 5G name.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Coverage, congestion, devices and distant services all affect what users feel.

content.prompt: A learner has 5G on their phone but a cloud demo still stutters indoors. What is a sensible explanation?

options.label: Indoor coverage, congestion or the remote service may still limit performance
5G always overrides every other limit automatically
The phone must be broken because 5G never varies
Cloud demos never use networks

feedback.correct: Correct. Even with 5G available, buildings, busy networks and remote services can still cause problems.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. 5G helps, but it does not remove every other cause of delay.

metadata.title: Apply: when could 5G help?

content.text: Apply: when could 5G help?
Think about mobile speed, many devices, or lower latency in suitable conditions. Pick a realistic situation and explain the benefit clearly.

content.prompt: Describe one situation where 5G could be useful and explain why. Mention speed, many devices, or latency in your answer.
content.guidance: A satisfactory answer names a clear situation (for example a busy games event, mobile multiplayer play, or many phones online) and explains the 5G benefit in plain English. Write at least 200 characters.

metadata.title: What is IPv6?
metadata.summary: Explain Internet Protocol version 6 and what an IP address does.

content.text: What is IPv6?

IPv6 means Internet Protocol version 6. An IP address is a numerical label that helps identify a device on a network so data can be sent to the right place, a bit like a postal address for a computer or phone.
Earlier networks often used IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4). IPv4 still works widely, but it has a limited supply of addresses. IPv6 provides a much larger address space.

content.title: Key term: address space
content.text: Address space means how many different IP addresses are available. A larger address space means more devices can have their own addresses.

content.prompt: What does an IP address mainly do?

options.label: It helps identify a device on a network so data can be delivered to the right place
It prints plastic models
It chooses the colour theme of a website only
It replaces the need for electricity

feedback.correct: Correct. An IP address helps route data to the correct device on a network.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Think of an IP address as a network label for finding a device.

content.prompt: What does IPv6 stand for?

options.label: Internet Protocol version 6
Instant Printer version 6
Indoor Painting varnish 6
In-game Points value 6

feedback.correct: Correct. IPv6 expands to Internet Protocol version 6.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Expand each letter: Internet Protocol version 6.

metadata.title: Why the internet needs more addresses
metadata.summary: Explain why growing numbers of devices make IPv6 important.

content.text: Why the internet needs more addresses
Phones, laptops, sensors, smart TVs and game consoles all need ways to join networks. As more devices come online, the internet needs more available IP addresses.
IPv6 matters because it provides a much larger supply of addresses than IPv4. That helps organisations and services that connect huge numbers of devices.

Example: an online gaming service may have millions of players' devices connecting over time. A company site may also have many staff devices, consoles and sensors. More addresses make that growth easier to manage.

content.prompt: Why does the internet need more available IP addresses?

options.label: Because the number of connected devices keeps growing
Because printers refuse to use paper
Because websites can only be blue
Because games cannot use controllers

feedback.correct: Correct. Growth in connected devices drives the need for more addresses.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Focus on the rising number of devices that need network identities.

content.prompt: How does IPv6 help compared with IPv4?

options.label: It provides a much larger address space
It deletes every older network forever
It means devices no longer need any identity
It only works for paper mail

feedback.correct: Correct. The main practical advantage for learners to remember is the much larger address space.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. IPv6 expands available addresses; it does not remove the need for device identity.

metadata.title: IPv6 is not just a faster internet
metadata.summary: Make clear that IPv6's main advantage is address supply and IP design, not raw speed alone.

content.text: IPv6 is not just a faster internet
It is easy to assume IPv6 simply means "faster internet". That is not the main point. Speed still depends on connections, devices and services.
IPv6's main advantage is the much larger supply of IP addresses, plus improvements to the way IP networking is designed. Organisations adopt it so growth in devices does not run out of addresses.

content.prompt: Which statement is correct?

options.label: IPv6 mainly provides a much larger address space; it is not simply a faster version of the internet
IPv6 always doubles every download speed worldwide with no other changes
IPv6 only changes the colour of status lights
IPv6 removes the need for any networks

feedback.correct: Correct. Focus on address supply and networking design, not a magic speed boost.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Do not treat IPv6 as only a speed upgrade.

content.prompt: A classmate says, "We need IPv6 so every page loads twice as fast." What should you reply?

options.label: Speed depends on many factors; the key IPv6 benefit is more IP addresses for more devices
Agree, because IPv6 always forces double speed
Agree, because IPv6 turns off every other protocol
Disagree, because IP addresses are never used online

feedback.correct: Correct. Challenge the speed-only claim and point back to address space.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Help your classmate focus on available addresses rather than guaranteed speed.

metadata.title: Apply: why might an organisation need IPv6?
metadata.summary: Explain why a growing organisation may need IPv6.

content.text: Apply: why might an organisation need IPv6?
Think about growth: more staff devices, more sensors, more player connections. Explain the need for more addresses in plain English.

content.prompt: Explain why a growing organisation may need IPv6. Mention IP addresses and connected devices in your answer.
content.guidance: A satisfactory answer says the organisation has more devices joining networks and needs a larger supply of IP addresses than older IPv4 addressing easily provides. Write at least 200 characters.

metadata.title: What is a blockchain?
metadata.summary: Describe blockchain as linked records shared across participants.

content.text: What is a blockchain?
A blockchain is a way of recording information in linked blocks. Each new block connects to earlier blocks, forming a chain of records.
Copies of a blockchain can be maintained across multiple computers or participants. That shared copy idea helps people check the same history rather than trusting only one private notebook.

content.title: Gaming example
content.text: Pixel Forge Games could record the ownership history of a digital item, such as a rare skin. Players and the studio could look back at who owned it over time.

content.prompt: Which statement best describes a blockchain?

options.label: Information recorded in linked blocks that can be shared across multiple participants
A single paper invoice locked in one drawer only
A 5G phone mast
A type of HDMI cable

feedback.correct: Correct. Linked blocks plus shared copies are the core Level 2 idea.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Focus on linked records that can be shared across participants.

content.prompt: Why might a game studio look at a blockchain record for a digital item?

options.label: To check the ownership history of that item over time
To print the item as a physical chair automatically
To replace the need for any game art
To turn the item into a WAN cable

feedback.correct: Correct. Ownership history is a clear example of what a shared record can show.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Think about verifying history, not printing furniture or changing cables.

metadata.title: How blockchain records are protected
metadata.summary: Explain cryptographic protection and why changing past records can be difficult.

content.text: How blockchain records are protected
Cryptographic techniques help protect records from unauthorised alteration. Cryptography here means mathematical methods that make tampering detectable.

Because blocks are linked, changing previously recorded information can be difficult. How difficult it is still depends on the blockchain's design and governance (the rules about who can approve changes).
Different blockchains can use different methods to agree on new blocks. Do not assume every blockchain works the same way or uses the same amount of energy.

content.prompt: How do cryptographic techniques help a blockchain?

options.label: They help protect records from unauthorised alteration and make tampering easier to detect
They guarantee every blockchain uses the same energy-heavy method
They delete the need for any rules or governance
They turn every record into a paper letter

feedback.correct: Correct. Cryptography supports integrity. Designs and energy use still vary.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Protection against unauthorised changes is the key point; methods are not all identical.

content.prompt: Why can changing an old blockchain entry be difficult?

options.label: Because blocks are linked and the design may make unauthorised rewrites hard to accept
Because blockchains never store any information
Because every blockchain is printed on paper once
Because IP addresses cannot exist on the same planet

feedback.correct: Correct. Linked blocks and rules make quiet rewrites harder, depending on design and governance.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Difficulty comes from linking and shared rules, not from having no data.

metadata.title: Blockchain uses and limitations
metadata.summary: Outline possible uses and balanced limitations without over-claiming.

content.text: Blockchain uses and limitations
Possible uses include tracking transactions, verifying the history of digital items, and recording supply-chain information (for example where a component came from).

Limitations can include energy use for some blockchain systems, transaction costs, performance, and the difficulty of correcting mistakes once records are accepted. Blockchain is one possible approach. It is not automatically the best solution for every game.

content.prompt: Which pair shows a possible use and a possible limitation?

options.label: Use: verify digital-item history; limitation: correcting mistakes can be difficult
Use: replace all electricity; limitation: blockchain never stores records
Use: print steel cars overnight; limitation: blockchains cannot use cryptography
Use: remove every network; limitation: games cannot have items

feedback.correct: Correct. History checking is a use; hard corrections are a realistic limitation.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Pick a genuine record-keeping use paired with a genuine drawback.

content.prompt: Pixel Forge is deciding whether to put every cosmetic item on a blockchain. Which judgement is best?

options.label: Blockchain is one option; the team should weigh benefits and limits rather than assume it is always best
Every game feature must use blockchain or it will fail
Blockchain never has any costs or limits
Blockchain always uses identical energy-heavy methods

feedback.correct: Correct. Treat blockchain as a choice to evaluate, not a default for every feature.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Avoid all-or-nothing claims. Designs and trade-offs vary.

metadata.title: Apply: benefit and limitation of blockchain ownership records
metadata.summary: Identify one benefit and one limitation of using blockchain for digital item ownership.

content.text: Apply: benefit and limitation
Use the Pixel Forge digital-item idea. Give one clear benefit and one clear limitation.

content.prompt: Identify one possible benefit and one limitation of using blockchain to record digital item ownership. Explain each briefly.
content.guidance: A satisfactory answer gives one benefit (for example shared ownership history that is harder to alter without detection) and one limitation (for example cost, performance, energy use for some systems, or difficulty correcting mistakes). Write at least 200 characters.

metadata.title: What is serverless computing?
metadata.summary: Define serverless computing and stress that servers still exist.

content.text: What is serverless computing?
Serverless computing means developers can run code or functions without managing individual servers themselves. The cloud provider manages much of the underlying server infrastructure.
Servers still exist. The word serverless does not mean an application has no servers. It means the team spends less time setting up and patching those servers day to day.

content.title: Note
content.text: Serverless computing does not mean "no computers". It means "you do not manage the servers yourself".

content.prompt: Which statement about serverless computing is correct?

options.label: Servers still exist, but the cloud provider manages much of the infrastructure while developers run code as functions
Serverless means the application truly uses zero computers anywhere
Serverless means every office must host its own physical rack
Serverless is another name for a paper form

feedback.correct: Correct. Servers remain; responsibility for much of the infrastructure shifts to the provider.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Do not take the word serverless literally as "no servers at all".

content.prompt: What can developers do in a serverless model?

options.label: Run code or functions without managing individual servers themselves
Avoid writing any application logic forever
Force every player to install a server under their desk
Delete the cloud provider's role completely

feedback.correct: Correct. Developers focus more on the code and less on day-to-day server care.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Serverless changes who manages servers, not whether code is needed.

metadata.title: How serverless responds to demand
metadata.summary: Explain scaling, benefits and limitations at Level 2.

content.text: How serverless responds to demand
Serverless computing can help applications respond to changing demand. When more events arrive, the provider can run more function instances. When demand drops, less capacity is needed.

Possible benefits include reduced infrastructure management and usage-based charging (paying for what runs). Limitations can include execution limits, costs that are hard to predict, and dependence on the cloud provider.

content.prompt: How can serverless computing help when demand changes?

options.label: The provider can run more or fewer function instances as events arrive
The application must stay at one fixed size forever
Demand changes are ignored by every cloud service
Players must reboot the whole internet manually

feedback.correct: Correct. Responding to changing demand is a core serverless benefit to outline.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Think about automatic capacity for short pieces of code as demand rises and falls.

content.prompt: Which pair correctly matches a benefit and a limitation?

options.label: Benefit: less day-to-day server management; limitation: dependence on the cloud provider
Benefit: zero computers exist; limitation: code never runs
Benefit: unlimited free execution forever; limitation: providers never matter
Benefit: no application logic needed; limitation: networks disappear

feedback.correct: Correct. Less management is a benefit; provider dependence is a real limitation.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Keep benefits and limits realistic.

metadata.title: Pixel Forge: a serverless reward function
metadata.summary: Use a game event example to show serverless code in practice.

content.text: Pixel Forge: a serverless reward function

Example: when a player completes a challenge, Pixel Forge Games could trigger a serverless function to process a reward. The function runs, updates the reward, and stops. The studio does not babysit a dedicated server for that small job all day.
If thousands of players finish at once, the provider can run many copies of that function. Quiet hours need far less capacity.

content.prompt: In the Pixel Forge example, what does the serverless function do?

options.label: It runs code to process a player reward when an event happens
It builds a physical prize machine in the office
It replaces the art team
It turns off all player accounts permanently

feedback.correct: Correct. A short function responds to an event without the team managing a whole server for that task.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Focus on event-driven code for a reward, not physical machines or staff replacement.

content.prompt: Why might this approach fit a game studio?

options.label: Reward events can spike; serverless can scale those short jobs without constant server care
Games never create events
Cloud providers refuse to run any code
Rewards must be calculated on paper only

feedback.correct: Correct. Spiky, short tasks are a classic fit for serverless functions.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Think about bursts of player events and reduced server management.

metadata.summary: Explain when serverless computing might help a game developer.

metadata.title: What is SD-WAN?
metadata.summary: Define WAN and Software-Defined Wide Area Network in plain English.

content.text: What is SD-WAN?
A wide area network (WAN) connects locations that are far apart, such as offices in different towns. SD-WAN means Software-Defined Wide Area Network.
SD-WAN uses software-based control to manage connections between different sites. An organisation might use broadband, fibre, or other available connections to link offices or locations.

content.title: Key idea
content.text: SD-WAN is about managing site-to-site networking with software. It does not automatically make every connection faster, and it does not remove the need for network security.

content.prompt: What does WAN stand for?

options.label: Wide area network
Weak app notebook
Wireless art number
Weekly activity note

feedback.correct: Correct. WAN expands to wide area network.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Wide area network is the expansion you need.

content.prompt: What does SD-WAN mean?

options.label: Software-Defined Wide Area Network
Super Digital Wallpaper And Notebook
Single Desktop Without Any Network
Secure Drawing With Acrylic Nibs

feedback.correct: Correct. SD-WAN expands to Software-Defined Wide Area Network.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Expand each part: Software-Defined Wide Area Network.

metadata.title: How organisations use SD-WAN
metadata.summary: Explain traffic management, monitoring and route selection at Level 2.

content.text: How organisations use SD-WAN
SD-WAN can help manage traffic, monitor connections, and select suitable routes between sites. Central software can apply policies instead of configuring every location by hand in the old way.

Possible benefits include centralised management and improved flexibility when choosing how sites connect. Limitations include setup costs, configuration complexity, dependence on available connections, and ongoing security requirements.

content.prompt: How can SD-WAN help an organisation?

options.label: By using software control to manage and monitor connections between sites and select suitable routes
By deleting the need for any network security
By guaranteeing every download is instant worldwide
By replacing every staff member with a cable

feedback.correct: Correct. Software-based control of site links is the core outline.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. SD-WAN helps manage connections; it does not remove security needs or create magic speed.

content.prompt: Which limitation should learners remember?

options.label: Setup cost, configuration complexity, dependence on available links, and security requirements still matter
SD-WAN has no costs or configuration work
SD-WAN never needs monitoring
SD-WAN only works on paper maps

feedback.correct: Correct. Benefits come with real-world limits and security duties.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Keep a balanced view of cost, complexity and security.

metadata.title: Pixel Forge: linking several locations
metadata.summary: Apply SD-WAN to a main office, studio and second business site.

content.text: Pixel Forge: linking several locations
Suppose Pixel Forge Games has a main office, a development studio and another business location. Staff need to share files, join calls and reach internal systems securely and reliably.

SD-WAN could help the company manage the links between those sites, watch connection health, and choose suitable routes using the broadband or fibre available at each place. Security controls are still required.

content.prompt: Why might Pixel Forge consider SD-WAN?

options.label: To manage network connections between multiple company locations more flexibly
To avoid connecting the sites at all
To replace game design with network cables
To guarantee that security is never needed again

feedback.correct: Correct. Multi-site connectivity is the scenario SD-WAN is designed to help with.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Focus on linking locations, not removing networks or security.

content.prompt: Which statement is most accurate for this scenario?

options.label: SD-WAN can help manage site links, but the company must still plan security and depend on available connections
SD-WAN automatically makes every connection the fastest possible with no planning
SD-WAN removes the studio from the network forever
SD-WAN only works if the company has a single laptop

feedback.correct: Correct. Flexibility helps, but security and real link quality still matter.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Avoid over-claiming speed or removing security duties.

metadata.title: Apply: why use SD-WAN across locations?
metadata.summary: Explain why a company with several locations might use SD-WAN.

content.text: Apply: why use SD-WAN across locations?
Mention multiple sites, software-based management of connections, and a realistic benefit such as flexibility or central control.

content.prompt: Explain why a company with several locations might use SD-WAN.

metadata.title: Welcome to Week 7

content.text: Welcome to Week 7
This week you outline drones, social media and vlogs. You then consolidate emerging technologies from Weeks 1 to 6 for Assessment Criterion (AC) 1.1.

content.title: By the end of this week
content.text: You will be able to say what drones, social media and vlogs are, give practical uses for each, and match earlier technologies to simple real-world examples. This is the last teaching week focused on AC1.1 before later learning outcomes.

Quick check from Week 6: 5G is fifth-generation mobile network technology. IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) mainly expands IP addresses. Blockchain records linked shared history. Serverless computing still uses servers, but the provider manages much of the infrastructure. SD-WAN (Software-Defined Wide Area Network) manages links between sites.

content.prompt: Which statement from Week 6 is correct?

options.label: Serverless computing means no computers exist anywhere
IPv6 mainly provides a much larger address space; it is not simply a faster internet
SD-WAN deletes the need for any network security
5G only works on paper maps

feedback.correct: Correct. IPv6 is mainly about address space, not a guaranteed speed boost.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Keep the Week 6 outlines in mind. IPv6 expands addresses. Serverless still uses servers.

content.prompt: What will you focus on this week for AC1.1?

options.label: Only spreadsheet formulas and paper filing
Drones, social media, vlogs, then consolidation of emerging technologies from earlier weeks

feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Read the welcome text again.

metadata.title: Linking earlier technologies
metadata.summary: Connect networks, cloud, AI and media ideas to this week's drones, social media and vlogs.

content.text: Linking earlier technologies
Drones can use cameras, sensors and wireless links. Social media and vlogs often run on cloud services and mobile networks. Artificial Intelligence (AI) may help recommend posts or edit video.
Pixel Forge Games already uses trailers, community posts and behind-the-scenes video. This week helps you outline those media tools alongside drones for promotional aerial clips.

content.prompt: Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: Drones, social media and vlogs never use any earlier digital technologies
These technologies often combine cameras, networks, cloud services and software ideas you already know
Cloud computing only works with paper letters
AI recommendations are identical to 3D printing

feedback.correct: Correct. New tools usually build on networks, devices and software you have already met.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Think about how media and drones use cameras, networks and cloud services.

content.prompt: Why might Pixel Forge care about this week?

options.label: Promotional footage, announcements and development diaries support player engagement
Games never use video or online communities
AC1.1 only covers printers

feedback.correct: Correct. Media and aerial clips can support marketing and community updates.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Focus on promotion and player communication.

metadata.title: What are drones?
metadata.summary: Define drones and Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) in plain English.

content.text: What are drones?
A drone is an aircraft that flies without a pilot on board. Many drones are also called Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs).

People often control drones from the ground with a remote controller or an app. Some drones can follow set routes more independently. You do not need deep engineering detail for AC1.1. Focus on what they are and what they are used for.

content.title: Key term: UAV
content.text: UAV means Unmanned Aerial Vehicle: an aircraft without a human pilot on board.

content.prompt: What is a drone in this unit?

options.label: An aircraft that flies without a pilot on board
A type of spreadsheet formula
A paper newsletter only
A blockchain wallet password

feedback.correct: Correct. Drones are unmanned aircraft, often called UAVs.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Keep the outline simple: aircraft without a pilot on board.

content.prompt: What does UAV stand for?

options.label: Unmanned Aerial Vehicle
Ultra Audio Volume
User Account Validation
Urban Art Venue

feedback.correct: Correct. UAV expands to Unmanned Aerial Vehicle.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Expand each letter: Unmanned Aerial Vehicle.

metadata.title: How drones operate
metadata.summary: Outline cameras, sensors, remote control, and manual versus more autonomous flight.

content.text: How drones operate
Many drones carry cameras or other sensors. Sensors collect information such as position, height or images. A remote control or mobile app lets an operator steer the drone.

Some flights are mainly manual, with a person steering carefully. Other modes are more autonomous, where the drone follows a planned path or tracks a subject with less constant stick input. Either way, a responsible operator still plans the flight.

content.prompt: What do drone cameras and sensors mainly do?

options.label: Collect images or other flight and environment data
Print plastic cases
Replace the need for electricity
Turn the drone into a spreadsheet

feedback.correct: Correct. Cameras and sensors gather useful data during flight.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Think about collecting images and flight information.

content.prompt: Which statement is accurate?

options.label: Drones can be steered manually or follow more automated routes, depending on the mode and design
Every drone always flies with no operator planning at all
Remote control is never used with drones
Autonomous always means the drone ignores all safety rules

feedback.correct: Correct. Control can be more manual or more automated, but planning still matters.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Operators still plan flights even when some modes are assisted.

metadata.title: Where drones are used
metadata.summary: Outline practical drone applications including Pixel Forge promotional footage.

content.text: Where drones are used
Drones are used for photography and film, delivery trials, agriculture surveys, inspections of roofs or towers, and some emergency-service views of hard-to-reach places.
Pixel Forge Games might use a drone to capture aerial footage of a launch event or outdoor promo shoot for a trailer, when rules and permissions allow it.

content.prompt: Which is a practical drone use?

options.label: Inspecting a tall structure safely from the air
Editing a spreadsheet with no camera
Sending only paper post with no aircraft
Turning off all wireless networks forever

feedback.correct: Correct. Inspections and aerial views are common practical uses.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Look for an aerial imaging or survey-style use.

content.prompt: How could Pixel Forge use a drone legally and carefully?

options.label: To film aerial promotional clips of an outdoor event when permissions allow
To ignore all privacy rules near people's homes
To replace every programmer with a flying camera
To delete the need for any game art

feedback.correct: Correct. Promotional aerial footage is a realistic studio use when done responsibly.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Focus on careful promotional filming, not rule-breaking.

metadata.title: Drone benefits, limits and safety
metadata.summary: Weigh advantages against safety, privacy and security considerations.

content.text: Drone benefits, limits and safety

Benefits include useful aerial views, reaching difficult places, and capturing footage that would be hard from the ground. Limitations include battery life, weather, cost, training needs and flight rules.
Safety, privacy and security matter. Operators must avoid harming people or property, respect private spaces, and follow local laws. A flying camera can raise privacy concerns if used carelessly.

content.prompt: Which pair correctly matches a benefit and a limitation?

options.label: Benefit: aerial views of hard-to-reach places; limitation: weather and battery life can restrict flights
Benefit: unlimited flight with no rules; limitation: drones never carry cameras
Benefit: no training ever needed; limitation: drones cannot fly outdoors
Benefit: privacy is never a concern; limitation: images cannot be stored

feedback.correct: Correct. Aerial access is useful; weather and batteries are real limits.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Pick a true benefit paired with a true limitation.

content.prompt: Why do privacy and safety matter for drone use?

options.label: Careless flights can risk people, property or private spaces
Privacy rules never apply to cameras
Safety only matters for paper planes
Drones cannot collect any images

feedback.correct: Correct. Responsible use protects people and respects privacy.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Think about harm, private spaces and responsible filming.

metadata.title: What is social media?
metadata.summary: Define social media platforms and how they support communication and sharing.

content.text: What is social media?
Social media platforms are online services where people create, share and discuss content. Examples include short-video apps, image feeds and community pages.
Social media has grown from simple status updates into rich media, live streams and business pages. Users communicate, follow creators and share news or entertainment.

content.prompt: What are social media platforms?

options.label: Online services where people create, share and discuss content
Only paper noticeboards in one office
Only offline board games
Only 3D printers

feedback.correct: Correct. Social media is about creating and sharing content online.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Focus on online sharing and discussion.

content.prompt: How has social media mainly evolved?

options.label: From simple updates toward richer media, communities and business use
By deleting the internet
By banning all images forever
By replacing electricity with candles only

feedback.correct: Correct. Platforms now support richer content and wider uses.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Think about growth in media types and communities.

metadata.title: Algorithms and recommendations
metadata.summary: Explain personalised recommendations in plain Level 2 language.

content.text: Algorithms and recommendations

An algorithm here means a set of rules or calculations used by software. Social media often uses algorithms to show personalised recommendations (posts the system predicts you may like based on what you watch, like or follow).
That can help people find useful content. It can also create filter bubbles or spread low-quality posts if users are not careful.

content.prompt: What do personalised recommendations mainly try to do?

options.label: Show content the system predicts the user may engage with
Print every post onto paper overnight
Turn off the user's device permanently
Replace the need for any network

feedback.correct: Correct. Recommendations try to match content to predicted interests.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Think about suggesting posts based on activity.

content.prompt: Which statement is balanced?

options.label: Recommendations can help discovery, but users should still think carefully about what they trust and share
Algorithms always show only perfect true information
Algorithms never affect what people see
Social media cannot show any video

feedback.correct: Correct. Useful discovery still needs careful judgement.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Keep benefits and risks in balance.

metadata.title: Personal and business uses of social media
metadata.summary: Outline marketing, engagement and Pixel Forge community examples.

content.text: Personal and business uses of social media
People use social media to stay in touch, share hobbies and follow news. Businesses use it for marketing, customer engagement and support.
Pixel Forge Games can announce releases, share trailers, collect community feedback and talk with players. Social media marketing means promoting a product or brand through these platforms.

content.prompt: Which is a business use of social media?

options.label: Sharing a game trailer and answering player questions on a studio page
Only writing on sticky notes with no digital tools
Turning off all player communication
Printing a network cable

feedback.correct: Correct. Announcements and engagement are common business uses.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Look for marketing or community communication.

content.prompt: What does customer engagement mean here?

options.label: Building ongoing interaction with customers or players through replies, posts and shared content
Never answering any message
Deleting every community page
Replacing players with paper forms only

feedback.correct: Correct. Engagement is about ongoing, two-way interaction.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Think about talking with and listening to players.

metadata.title: Social media benefits, limits and safety
metadata.summary: Cover benefits plus privacy, misinformation and online safety.

content.text: Social media benefits, limits and safety
Benefits include wide reach, fast updates and community building. Limitations include time cost, negative comments, platform rule changes and uneven reach.

Privacy, misinformation and online safety matter. Misinformation means false or misleading information presented as if it were true. Users and studios should protect personal data, check sources and behave respectfully.

content.prompt: What is misinformation?

options.label: False or misleading information presented as if it were true
A type of drone propeller
A cloud storage folder name only
A printer ink colour

feedback.correct: Correct. Misinformation is false or misleading content.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Focus on false or misleading information.

content.prompt: Which safety practice is sensible for Pixel Forge staff?

options.label: Protect account access, avoid sharing private personal data, and check facts before posting
Post every password in public comments
Ignore all privacy settings forever
Assume every viral claim is automatically true

feedback.correct: Correct. Protect accounts, privacy and accuracy.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Choose responsible online behaviour.

metadata.title: What is a vlog?
metadata.summary: Define vlogs and contrast them with blogs.

content.text: What is a vlog?
A vlog is a video blog: regular video updates shared online. A blog is usually written text posts. Both can inform or entertain, but a vlog uses video as the main format.
Creators film, edit and upload episodes. Viewers watch on social platforms or video sites.

content.prompt: What is a vlog?

options.label: A video blog: regular video updates shared online
A paper-only diary locked in a drawer
A type of UAV propeller
A spreadsheet formula

feedback.correct: Correct. Vlog means video blog.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Focus on regular video updates shared online.

content.prompt: How does a vlog mainly differ from a typical blog?

options.label: A vlog centres on video; a typical blog centres on written text
A vlog can never be shared online
A blog always requires a drone
They are identical in every way

feedback.correct: Correct. The main difference is video versus written posts.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Compare video format with written posts.

metadata.title: Creating and sharing video content
metadata.summary: Outline equipment, software, streaming and recorded video.

content.text: Creating and sharing video content
Common equipment includes a camera or phone, microphone and lighting. Software is used to edit clips, add titles and export a finished file.
Recorded video is filmed first, then edited and uploaded later. Streaming means sending video live as it happens. Both can support tutorials or studio updates.

content.prompt: What is the difference between streaming and recorded video?

options.label: Streaming is live as it happens; recorded video is filmed first and shared later
Streaming always means printing DVDs
Recorded video can never be edited
They both require a drone by law

feedback.correct: Correct. Live versus filmed-then-uploaded is the key difference.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Think about live broadcast versus later upload.

content.prompt: Why might creators use editing software?

options.label: To cut clips, add titles and prepare a clearer finished video
To delete the need for any camera
To turn video into a WAN cable
To replace electricity

feedback.correct: Correct. Editing improves clarity and presentation.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Editing shapes the finished video.

content.text: Vlogs for games and studios
Personal uses include sharing hobbies and daily stories. Business uses include tutorials, product demos and behind-the-scenes updates.

Gaming content creators and studios often publish development diaries, tutorials and promotional videos. Pixel Forge could film short diary episodes about a feature build, then upload them to engage players.

options.label: Creators should not use other people's protected work without permission
Copyright only applies to paper books from 1800

metadata.title: Welcome to Week 8
metadata.summary: Introduce AC2.1 personal and business uses. Recap that Weeks 1 to 7 already outlined the technologies.

content.text: Welcome to Week 8

This week you explain personal and business uses of emerging technologies for Assessment Criterion (AC) 2.1. You already outlined what many technologies are in Weeks 1 to 7. Now you focus on how people and organisations use them.

content.title: AC1.1 versus AC2.1
content.text: AC1.1 is about identifying and outlining technologies. AC2.1 is about explaining how those technologies are used in personal and business contexts.

Quick reminder of tools you already met: Artificial Intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IoT), cloud computing, Virtual Reality (VR), Augmented Reality (AR), 5G, social media, vlogs, drones, blockchain and serverless computing.

content.prompt: What is the main focus of AC2.1 in this week?

options.label: Explaining personal and business uses of emerging technologies
Memorising every chip voltage inside a drone
Writing a full company investment case with no uses
Ignoring all real-world examples

feedback.correct: Correct. AC2.1 asks you to explain uses in personal and business contexts.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. This week is about how technologies are used, not deep engineering or investment analysis.

content.prompt: How does AC2.1 differ from AC1.1?

options.label: AC1.1 outlines what technologies are; AC2.1 explains how they are used by people and organisations
They are identical and only rename the same task
AC2.1 only means drawing cables
AC1.1 only covers social media passwords

feedback.correct: Correct. First identify/outline, then explain uses.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Keep identification separate from explaining uses.

metadata.title: Personal use and business use
metadata.summary: Define personal and business technology use and show that one technology can serve both.

content.text: Personal use and business use
Personal use means an individual uses technology for their own life: entertainment, learning, health, communication or home tasks.
Business use means an organisation uses technology to run or grow its work: serving customers, making products, marketing, collaborating or analysing performance.
The same technology can do both. AI can recommend music at home and also power customer support at Pixel Forge Games.

content.prompt: Which example is mainly personal use?

options.label: A player uses a VR headset at home for leisure gaming
A studio runs AI tools to analyse thousands of support tickets
A warehouse tracks stock with IoT sensors for deliveries
A marketing team posts trailers to grow sales

feedback.correct: Correct. Home leisure gaming is personal use.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Personal use is for an individual's own life, not studio operations.

content.prompt: Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: One technology can have personal uses and business uses depending on the purpose
Every technology can only ever have one use forever
Business use means the technology has no users
Personal use always means unpaid work for a company

feedback.correct: Correct. Purpose and context decide personal versus business use.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Focus on who is using it and why.

metadata.title: From outline to use
metadata.summary: Bridge AC1.1 outlines into AC2.1 use explanations with short examples.

content.text: From outline to use

Earlier weeks asked what a technology is. This week asks what it is used for. Example: IoT is connected devices; a personal use is a smart speaker at home; a business use is tracking studio equipment.
Keep explanations short: name the technology, state the purpose, and say whether the user is a person or an organisation.

content.prompt: Which answer shows an AC2.1-style use explanation?

options.label: Cloud computing is used by Pixel Forge to host shared build files for remote artists
Cloud
Technology exists
Emerging

feedback.correct: Correct. The sentence explains a clear organisational use.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. AC2.1 needs purpose and context, not only a label.

content.prompt: Which pair is correctly framed?

options.label: Outline: what VR is; use: staff training in a headset at Pixel Forge
Outline and use are the same single word with no example
Use explanations are banned in AC2.1
Only costs belong in AC2.1

feedback.correct: Correct. Separate the outline from the use.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Keep identification and use explanations distinct.

metadata.title: Personal uses: AI and IoT
metadata.summary: Explain everyday personal uses of AI assistants/recommendations and IoT devices.

content.text: Personal uses: AI and IoT
Personal AI uses include virtual assistants that answer questions or set reminders, and recommendation systems that suggest music, videos or games.
Personal IoT uses include smart home devices (lights, thermostats) and wearables that track steps or heart rate. The point for AC2.1 is the use, not redesigning the hardware.

content.prompt: Which is a personal AI use?

options.label: A phone assistant recommends playlists based on listening habits
A factory robot only packing boxes for shop orders
A studio blockchain ledger for digital item ownership history
An SD-WAN link between two offices

feedback.correct: Correct. Personal recommendations and assistants are everyday AI uses.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Look for an individual's everyday AI helper or recommendations.

content.prompt: Which is a personal IoT use?

options.label: A fitness watch sharing activity data with the wearer's phone
A company tracking every delivery van for logistics only
A marketing team scheduling ad campaigns
A serverless function processing studio reward events

feedback.correct: Correct. Wearables for personal health or fitness are personal IoT uses.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Personal IoT is about an individual's connected devices.

metadata.title: Personal uses: cloud, VR and AR
metadata.summary: Outline personal cloud storage/apps and immersive entertainment or navigation uses.

content.text: Personal uses: cloud, VR and AR
Personal cloud computing uses include storing photos, backing up phone files and opening apps through a browser or client.
Personal VR uses include immersive games and experiences. Personal AR uses include navigation overlays or interactive filters that add digital information to the real world.

content.prompt: Which is a personal cloud use?

options.label: Backing up personal photos so they can be opened on another device
Hosting Pixel Forge's entire multiplayer backend for all players
Linking three studios with SD-WAN only
Inspecting a roof with a drone for a client

feedback.correct: Correct. Personal backups and file access are cloud uses for individuals.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Focus on an individual's storage or apps.

content.prompt: Which pair correctly matches a personal use?

options.label: VR for immersive home gaming; AR for street navigation overlays
VR only for printing plastic; AR only for office WAN routing
VR and AR only for unpaid staff rotas
VR means social media passwords

feedback.correct: Correct. Gaming and navigation are clear personal immersive uses.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Match VR/AR to everyday individual experiences.

metadata.title: Personal uses: 5G, social media and vlogs
metadata.summary: Explain personal mobile connectivity and content creation/communication uses.

content.text: Personal uses: 5G, social media and vlogs
Personal 5G uses include faster mobile communication and smoother cloud gaming on a phone when coverage and conditions allow.
Personal social media and vlog uses include chatting with friends, following creators and making video diaries for a hobby audience.

content.prompt: Which is a personal 5G use?

options.label: Playing a cloud game on a phone while travelling, where 5G coverage is good
A studio using SD-WAN to link finance and art offices
A warehouse IoT system counting pallets
A company blockchain for supply-chain records

feedback.correct: Correct. Mobile cloud gaming/communication for an individual is a personal 5G use.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Look for an individual's mobile connectivity benefit.

content.prompt: Which is mainly personal media use?

options.label: A learner posts a hobby vlog about their weekend projects
Pixel Forge's marketing team running a paid launch campaign
Customer support analysing ticket trends with AI
Drones inspecting company buildings on a contract

feedback.correct: Correct. A personal hobby vlog is individual use.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Business marketing and operations are not personal use.

content.text: Business uses: AI, IoT and cloud
Business AI uses include customer support chat tools and data analysis that helps teams spot patterns in sales or player behaviour.
Business IoT uses include monitoring assets and tracking equipment or shipments. Business cloud uses include team collaboration, hosting services and secure backups.

content.text: Support staff can use AI-assisted replies, while cloud tools host builds and let remote artists share files.

metadata.title: Business uses: VR, AR and drones
metadata.summary: Outline training, demos, development and promotional/inspection uses.

content.text: Business uses: VR, AR and drones
Business VR/AR uses include staff training, product demonstrations and game development reviews where teams test immersive scenes.
Business drone uses include photography, site inspections and promotional aerial content when permissions allow.

metadata.title: Business uses: social media, blockchain and serverless
metadata.summary: Explain marketing, records and event-driven application uses.

content.text: Business uses: social media, blockchain and serverless
Business social media uses include marketing and customer engagement: trailers, announcements and replies to players.

Business blockchain uses can include transaction records or digital asset ownership history. Serverless computing can run event-driven tasks, such as processing a reward when a player completes a challenge, without the team managing every server day to day.

Deleting every cloud service forever

feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Focus on organisational event code and reduced server management.

metadata.title: Pixel Forge: development, testing and support
metadata.summary: Explain technology uses for building games and helping players.

content.text: Pixel Forge: development, testing and support
During development and testing, cloud collaboration helps share builds. VR/AR can support immersive playtests. AI can help triage bug reports.
For player support, AI-assisted tools can suggest answers, while social media and help desks collect feedback. The AC2.1 skill is explaining the use, not listing tool brands.

content.prompt: How might cloud computing help Pixel Forge development?

options.label: By letting remote teammates share and back up project files online

By removing the need for any game design
By turning off all player accounts automatically

feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Focus on shared files and teamwork.

options.label: By analysing common questions and suggesting helpful replies for staff
By flying a drone instead of answering tickets
By deleting all feedback forever
By replacing 5G coverage maps with paper only

feedback.correct: Correct. Support analysis and suggested replies are business AI uses.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Link AI to understanding and answering player needs.

metadata.title: Pixel Forge: multiplayer, marketing and analytics
metadata.summary: Explain uses for online services, promotion and understanding players.

content.text: Pixel Forge: multiplayer, marketing and analytics
Online multiplayer often relies on cloud hosting and strong mobile or broadband links (including 5G for players on the move). Serverless functions can handle spikes such as reward claims.
Marketing uses social media and sometimes drone or video content. Game analytics may use AI or data tools to understand how players behave so the team can improve the experience.

content.prompt: Which explanation best describes a multiplayer-related use?

options.label: Cloud hosting keeps multiplayer services available to many players at once
Multiplayer only works on paper leaderboards
Marketing posts replace the need for any servers
Analytics means deleting all player feedback

feedback.correct: Correct. Hosting capacity is a clear business cloud use for multiplayer.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Think about how online services stay available.

content.prompt: How can social media and analytics work together for Pixel Forge?

options.label: Social posts promote the game; analytics helps the team understand player behaviour and responses
Analytics removes the need for any marketing
Social media cannot collect any public comments
Both tools only exist for home lighting

feedback.correct: Correct. Promotion and insight are complementary business uses.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Separate the marketing use from the insight use, then link them.

metadata.title: Pixel Forge: remote teamwork and player feedback
metadata.summary: Explain cloud and social/AI uses for remote work and listening to players.

content.text: Pixel Forge: remote teamwork and player feedback
Remote teamwork often uses cloud applications for calls, documents and shared storage so staff in different places can work together.
Player feedback can arrive through social media comments, surveys or support tickets. AI tools may help group similar comments so the team can respond and improve the game.

content.prompt: How does cloud computing support remote teamwork?

options.label: Staff can open shared files and collaborate online from different locations
Remote teamwork never needs any digital tools
Cloud means only flying drones outdoors
Cloud deletes all player feedback

Because AC2.1 forbids examples
